speechtext: Is my hon. friend advocating an aeroplane station or a hydroplane station for Oape Breton island?

Probably a hydroplane station would be the better. That, of course, is a matter that experts would have

to decide. I am not an expert in either branch myself. We shall not, however, quarrel on that phase .of the subject.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: The distinction is a very important one.

Perhaps I have taken up more time than I intended when I started to speak on this very important subject. I feel that a fair discussion should take place on it and I feel that the Government will not be doing their duty unless they take the matter up in an energetic manner and do something tangible that will tend to offset the menace with whicn the cause of tiie Empire and of the Allies is threatened at the present time.

Mr. Speaker, I would like to make one remark on this subject. I have already expressed my opinion in this. House as to the construction of all possible ships, and at this late hour, Canada in conjunction with the United States can not build too many transports and commercial ships.
Every time I see a report that one of our ships has been sunk by a submarine I regret that the ship has gone to the bottom, but I still more deeply regret the food that has gone down with her. If the Germans increase their submarine activities it may be that after a certain length of time we shall be left without ships to transport our food. The hon. gentleman who has just sat down has drawn attention to the fact that during the last three weeks thirteen Austrian submarines have been sunk in the Mediterranean by the Italian navy. Great Britain and the United States are combatting the submarine not only by replacing the ships that are lost, but by directly destroying the submarines themselves by means of destroyers of all kinds. If the view of my right hon. leader in 1911, that small vessels and destroyers should be built in this country, had been acted upon, it would have been of immense value in meeting the attacks of the German submarines. Italy is the best equipped of all the Allied navies, in proportion to her total strength, in the matter of small destroyers of all kinds. The war has shown that vessels of this kind are most important. While I would urge the Canadian Government to do everything possible in the way of building merchant ships, both steel and wood, they should also build destroyers to attack the submarines. It is quite possible that more good would be done by sinking ten or twelve submarines

than by building an equal number of commercial vessels to replace the tonnage that has been sunk. My purpose in rising was to call the attention of the acting Prime Minister to this very important consideration.
Mr. D- D. McKENZIE (North Cape Breton):	The question that is before us
to-day is by no means a new one, and if it had been discussed this afternoon in an acrimonious partisan way, I do not think I should have taken part in the discussion, as I would regard the time as inopportune for discussing a question of this great importance from the standpoint of paTty politics. I am glad that every hon. gentleman who has spoken on the question this afternoon has avoided as much as possible the introduction of keen party spirit. I was pleased and proud to hear the very able speech of the hon. member for Pictou (Mr. Macdonald). We have heard him often on various questions, but I do not know that I ever heard him to better advantage than this afternoon. It is true to say that I never before heard the question of naval affairs .so ably presented in this House except on one occasion, the speech on that particular occasion transcended everything that has ever been heard in this House or perhaps ever will be. The honour and glory of putting the case in that admirable way belongs to the right hon. gentleman who to-day leads the Government (Sir George Foster). On the 29th of March 1909 we heard him present this case in a way that could not be excelled, and this afternoon I wish to remind him-I say remind, because Paul when writing to some of his people was so delicate and careful in his language that he did not like to say they were bad, so he simply reminded them that there were certain things which they had acknowledged and of their duty in that regard-I simply wish to remind the right hon. gentleman of that celebrated and famous speech of his, perhaps the best in his career of many able speeches, in which he laid down the principles which actuated himself and which should actuate the Government in regard to naval affairs. If the Government of which he is a distinguished member would only carry out in a small way the principle.! which he then advocated my hon. friend from Pictou and the rest of us would be amply rewarded for any efforts we have made this afternoon. It is quite unnecessary for me to take up any time in pointing out the necessity for some action being taken. The 85
necessity lias been clearly demonstrated; indeed, it was not necessary for it to be demonstrated, fox we all knew it. The hon. member for Pictou did not bring this matter up to-day, and we are not making these speeches, because we think there is anybody in this country who does not fully realize the great necessity of taking steps to protect this country. Our object is simply to stir up the Government to speedy action.
It may be said, although I do not think it is strong ground to take now, that the Government might fear adverse criticism from this side of the House, but we are disarming ourselves by throwing everything into the pot, -so to speak, -and giving to the Government the full weight and authority of whatever arguments we put forward, and our sympathy and support of any action taken by them along this line. As I said before, this is not a new question. When the present Minister of Naval Affairs addressed this House for the first time as a member of the present Government he said, speaking on this very question (Hansard Nov. 22, 1911):
I think the people of this country will approve of the action of this Government in hesitating before rushing hastily into a policy which must involve an expenditure of so many million dollars every year. I think they will appreciate the course of this Government in doing what was stated by the Prime Minister in his admirable speech in reply to the right hon. leader of the Opposition, when he said it was the intention of the Government to consider with the English Admiralty this whole naval question -from first to last. When we have done that, I think we will be able to come before this House and this country with a policy that will appeal to all Canadians as a policy that will he the best for the people of Canada and the best in the interest of the Empire in which we live.
That is getting -to be quite a while ago now. That speech was delivered on the 22nd d-ay of November, 1911, when there was no war in sight. The Minister of Naval Affairs said that the matter was under consideration, that they were going to take it up with the British Admiralty, and that a policy would be evolved that would be satisfactory to the Canadian people. I am impelled to say that in at least on-e respect this Government bears a semblance of divine grace, for on-e day is to them as a thousand years, and a thousand years but as one day. They were going to start immediately. But now it i-s pretty well on to six years since this plan was made, and there is not a ripple upon the surface to indicate any action on their part. I hope this debate



will be the means of stirring them up. I realize that the Prime Minister (Sir Robert Borden) is not here, that the Minister of Naval Affairs (Mr. Hazen) is not here. Still, we have an Administration and "the King's business must go on." I trust that the Acting Prime Minister (Sir George Foster) and the Acting Minister of Naval Affairs (Mr. Reid), knowing that there will be no opposition to any proper action on their part, will take courage, will gird up their loins, and will do. something for the protection of the country and the advancement of our merchant marine.
How this shall be done is a matter for these hon. gentlemen to propose. I would suggest that we have in this country great concerns that, war or no war, will require many ships, and that it might be a good plan to associate these concerns with the Government in shipbuilding. Take, for instance, the Canadian Pacific Railway. The great transportation requirements of that concern make it necessary for them to use many ships. If they could be induced to undertake shipbuilding in this country, with the capital at their command, the facilities they enjoy and their great connections, their co-operation would be of the greatest advantage, and their interest in the matter would be a guarantee that, war or no war, the vessels would be used. There is in my own county and in that of my hon. friend from South Cape Breton (Mr. Carroll) a great concern, the Dominion Steel and Coal Company, Ltd. They require a great number of ships, and if the Government could enlist their co-operation in shipbuilding it would be a great advantage to the country. Another company which has its headquarters in Sydney Harbour is the Nova Scotia Steel and Coal Company, which is much in the same position, and which is now actually engaged in building ships. It is not as large a concern as the others I have mentioned, but a large concern nevertheless, and the men connected with it are men of vision in the affairs of the country. But, even should these people refuse to engage in this business, we have money of our own, and this Parliament is ready to vote for these purposes any reasonable sum. We have plenty of talent in Canada to enable us to build these ships. I understand that in Montreal-there is already a shipyard which can turn out destroyers. The minister should take the full power of that concern for our own purposes, so far as the naval part of it is concerned.
As to wooden shipbuilding, every creek and cove along the Atlantic coast in New

Brunswick and Nova Scotia is a potential shipyard, and shipbuilding in these places can be encouraged. The Government of Nova Scotia is starting in that direction, and I hope that this Government will cooperate with them or any other provincial government that will move effectively along business lines in this important matter. I trust that the Government will be stimulated to such action as will result in the solution of this problem so far as our own interests are concerned and will enable ns to give assistance to the Empire which shall be a worthy expression of the ambition and pride of Canadians.

It is universally admitted that we face a crisis in the history of the world and a crisis in the history of Canada because of the scarcity of ships. While present conditions exist our trans-Atlantic trade will be injured, and our interprovincial trade as well. One factor that has caused scarcity of Canadian shipping is the Norwegian-built and Norwegian-manned ship which for many years has received and is still receiving all the privileges of our coasting trade while not subject to restrictions put upon British and Canadian ships. For instance, British ships that are condemned can be purchased by Norwegians, they can be manned more cheaply, and outfitted more cheaply in Norway than in Britain or in Canada, and they are given all the coasting privileges of this country. The competition of these vessels has been so keen that the Canadian flag has been practically driven off the water. That should have been prevented, or at least considered. But now
5 p.m. we are confronted with a condition under which our transatlantic trade and our interprovincial trade will be handicapped unless the scarcity of ships is remedied. And it seems to me that this cannot be remedied under present circumstances unless the Government comes to the assistance either of corporations or private concerns which take up the building of ships. The Newfoundland Government has grappled with this question. There was a scarcity of shipping there such as in Canada. I understand that the Government there is giving a bonus of $20 a ton on wooden ships. And it is stated by those who have some knowledge of this subject that $20 a ton bonus would be sufficient to induce men with capital, men of experience, to undertake the building of wooden vessels in the Maritime Provinces. Years ago, the industry of building wooden

ships was a very important one in the Maritime Provinces, but owing to conditions which I need not mention, for they are known to everybody, wooden ships practically disappeared from the seas, except ships flying the Norwegian flag.
At present, and while the war is on, the Government, no doubt, has to consider carefully the ways and means. I have a suggestion to make on that point which may be worthy of consideration. The Government has now oh the Order Paper notice of a Bill standing in the name of the Minister of Railways (Mr. Cochrane) "An Act to encourage and assist the improvement of highways." I understand that it is the intention of the Government to appropriate $10,000,000 for this purpose. That, I think, is a matter that is not nearly so pressing at this time as the construction of ships. I think it will be a contentious and controversial measure.
I doubt the propriety of the Government introducing highly controversial legislation at this time and under the prevailing circumstances. If the Government would devote to shipbuilding the $10,000,000 proposed to be spent under this Act, if it is passed, it would meet with the general approval of the House and the people of Canada. If $20 a ton is sufficient to attract capital, skill and labour, in the colony of Newfoundland, perhaps a similar amount would he sufficient to attract capital, labour and machinery for the construction of ships in this country. I say that $20 a ton would build 500,000 tons of shipping, a very considerable quantity, that would probably meet all the needs of Canada for some years to come. The question of building standardized ships for ocean transportation, of course, would have to be considered and would likely be considered in connection with this subject. But the question of building smaller ships that could take part in the inteTprovineial trade, which is just as important as the trans-Atlantic trade and should not be overlooked. The building of smaller ships would establish ian important industry and these ships would be useful as feeders to the trans-Atlantic trade. The industry would not only give employment to the mechanics who were building the ships, but employment to the carrying trade which at the present time is in a serious position in the Maritime Provinces. We have not the ships or the coasting schooners to-day to do the trade which is so essential in that part of the country. It is going to be a serious matter for the people living along the coast, where there is no railway
85j
communication, to carry on the ordinary business of the country. It is certainly a matter that the Government should take into consideration. The amount necessary to meet the conditions is well within the resources of Canada. I would again urge upon the Government the advisability of considering whether or not this more pressing need might not be taken in hand before they proceed with the Highways Bill which stands on the Order Paper. I wished to make these remarks on this question because it is the most pressing question which Canada has to face to-day, and a most important question to the whole of Canada, and particularly to the people who dwell upon the coast, of British Columbia and the Maritime Provinces. I hope the Government will make an announcement on this subject.

Mr. Speaker, my hon. friend from Piiotou (Mr. Macdonald) has certainly taken generous advantage of the provision, of the rules of the House under which he has made the motion. I do not think I would be travelling outside of the record if I stated that this particular rule wae framed for the purpose of giving facility for discussing on sudden emergencies very urgent questions, which the ordinary leisurely rules of the House would not permit. I do not think it was ewer meant that this rule was ito be used as a channel by which discussions were to be brought on without regular notice, upon subjects of general policy such as this, and which hare been before the House again and again and again. The statement of my hon. friend'-I aim just making this criticism by way of commencement-upon which; he gets his opportunity to address the House; and initiate this discussion is that he desires :
-to discuss a definite matter of urgent public importance, namely, the menace to national interests by the German submarine campaign and the necessity of meeting it, and what Canada should do to deal with the situation.
On any fair interpretation of the rule, that would mean that there had rapidly developed in the mind of my hon. friend such urgency in reference to submarine warfare that he could not wait on the general rule which allows debate in the ordinary parliamentary way. In so far as my hon. friend kept himself to the discussion of the submarine peril, and to what we should do to grapple with it and destroy it, he was entirely within intention of the rule he

invoked, and so far I have no objection to
find.
But this is really a very delicate question to launch into the House for general discussion. The hon. gentleman (Mr. Macdonald) says that such-and-such is in peril; that we are doing nothing to counteract it, or, he asks: What are you doing to counteract it? To defend ourselves against such an attack, I would have to detail to the House just exactly what has been and what is being done, which, of course, it is impossible to do if we are to exercise common-sense prudence in this war time. One hon. gentleman opposite detailed to the House that there were certain localities in the Maritime Provinces where there was absolutely no protection, and where there are banks filled with money. The Kaiser has long ears, as it has not taken the world three years to discover. He gets information, and so do his minions, all the world over. If you should make sufficient answer to the man who tells you that this is a peril and that you have done nothing against it, you would have to say just where the strong points are and what they are, and thus advertise to the German Government that these are the points that they have to avoid; or if one points out that there are defenceless places which could be easily attacked, the German Government would be very glad to know. Their submarines sail under the sea, they are hidden from human ken, and information of this kind would doubtless help them in the effectiveness of their operations.
So that it is a delicate matter to take into a legislature. Much criticism has been made in Britain-some of it perhaps fairly just, much of it certainly unjust-as to the amount of publicity which should be given to those matters, and there have been heated discussions on it in the Houses of Parliament and outside. But that there is danger in public revelations of what is being done, no member opposite will deny. If I understood my hon. friend, his plea was that the transports for troops and munitions and food provisions that went from Canada were in peril because there was not sufficient provision for defence against possible disaster from submarines; and if I caught one sentence of his aright, it was to the effect that these transports went over without being properly convoyed. Now, not a transport has left a Canadian port which has not been under the supervision, under the direction, under the ^guidance of the British Admiralty, from
I Sir George Foster.]
the time it started until it reached its destination, and the British Admiralty commands the greatest naval force and facilities of any country in the world, as great as almost all other countries combined. It is not fair to create the impression amongst the people of the country, a great many of whom naturally enough do not have the facilities for understanding these questions, that our troops and our supplies for the troops are really passing across the sea in peril and ungarded because the Canadian Government has not done thus and so. My hon. friend speaks about the Deutschland having come over to this side of the ocean. We all know that there are possibilities. The U boat of the present time is a wonderful ingenious machine of great power and of wide scope as to the zone of its operations. It is a peril, but nobody will, deny that the peril of the submarine has up to the present been and even at the present time is mainly on the other side of the Atlantic and not on this side, so that the defensive and offensive machinery against the submarine have been put into force where they are moist effective and are most largely called for. There is a peril on this side of the Atlantic, but if. is a possible peril rather than an extremely probable one, and it is one which, if probable, is not at all the serious peril that it is on the other side of the Atlantic. I can not go into detail because it would not be wise to do so, although I know that some will say: "Oh, that is a subterfuge." It is not meant as a subterfuge at all. I am absolutely honest in making that statement. It is impossible for me or for any member of the Government to go into the matter before the House and to show to the hon. member for Pictou (Mr. Macdonald) and the other members of the House just what has been done and what is being done in order to protect our Atlantic coast from the peril of the submarine, probable only although it be.
Does this statement relate to what is done by this Government or by the British Government?

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: In this matter the Canadian Government does not feel that it is incumbent on it to look after the whole naval protection of this side of the Atlantic ocean any more than it feels that it is incumbent on it to look after all the land forces and power necessary to secure a successful conclusion of the war. It does not arrogate to itself that duty. It works in conjunction and complete and close

speakerposition: topic
stagedirection
speechtext:
unity with the Government of Great Britain, and the naval and military authorities of Great Britain; and every step that we have taken, and every step that we have avoided, has been taken or avoided after consultation with and on the advice of the British Government, through its admiralty and navy. My hon. friend need not be in too much trepidation as to what has been done and is now being done and will be done for the protection of these coasts. I can not go into particulars, but I may say to my hon. friend that to-day every ship-yard in the Dominion of Canada which is able to build ships and has an equipment therefor, has not only the opportunity but has the actual contract for building every craft that it can possibly build; that to-day the building of vessels in this country for the specific purpose of warding off and fighting against the submarine peril is engaging the activities, is employing the labour, and is being carried out by the supervision of the ship yards in this country. The statement I made a moment ago covers the whole ground.
As to wooden ships, an arrangement is now completed and is being carried out whereby anybody or any company that can undertake in 'a bona fide way to build wooden ships and tc deliver them within a certain time, will get the opportunity of building the ships ajid will be assured that the ship will pay for the cost of construction, with a reasonable profit. That is being done along the line of the co-operation that I have spoken of. We are working together, in and in with each other. These ships and vessels-let me be perfectly frank about it-are being financed in the main by British capital but they are being helped as well by the Dominion Government, and the operative work is being done by 'Canadian labour under Canadian supervision. So if the position is taken that the problem of meeting the submarine peril includes the finding of finished ships to fill the shortage of tonnage that has been caused by the submarine destruction, we can say that everything is being done that can be done in Canada to-day, taking into account possible labour, possible material, and ship building equipment. Every ship that can be made in Canada is being constructed as rapidly as possibly can be in order to help to fill the shortage of tonnage caused by the submarine destruction-If what the hon. gentleman (Mr. Macdonald) is looking for in the first place is, that, the submarine peril shall 'be met and
grappled with, then it is being met and grappled with. If what the hon. gentleman has in his mind is that, if the submarine continues to put a large number of ships to the bottom, the shortage shall be made good as speedily as possible-that is being grappled with. It will be met by the construction of British ships with British money, many of which are being built to-day and will be built this year and next year in Canada.
Are they to be Canadian registry ships, or are they not?

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: My hon. friend is acute and shrewd. There was no need for that question, because I said as ex-plicity as the King's English could put it that these ships were being built by British capital.

Then you are not
doing anything in the matter of building: ships.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: Whom does the hon. gentleman mean by "you"?
The Government.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext:
What is the
special anxiety o.f my hon. friend? Is it as to the work which he says he wants done, being done under British capital expenditure, and in British dominions, of which this country is one? Is that what he is after when he looks upon conditions resulting from the submarine war and expresses a desire that its ravages shall be repaired? If that isi what he is afteT, be has a sufficient answer-that is being done. Or does he want to launch the accusation against the Canadian Government that they aTe not putting their own money into this; that they are not doing it with theiT own particular means? Does he say: I acknowledge that that accusation, even if well founded, has been fully met by provision for reparation to the extent that we can make it with British capital in this country, but I want to make a case against the Government itself and so it does not satisfy me that the void is being filled; I want it filled by you, and because you do not fill it, I shall have a grievance. He asks for leadership. Is the member for Pictou a heaven-born leader? Is he erecting himself into a naval and military critic who knows more about what ought to be done on this coast with aeroplanes, with submarines, and with all the machinery for coast protection, than do the British Admiralty, with their brave and

skilful officers, and with their centuries of experience? My hon. friend may be justified from a party point of view, but hon. gentlemen will have observed that he told us he started out with the idea of saying nothing in a partisan spirit. It was his immense apprehension of the submarine peril and his immense desire that that peril should be met and that the vacuum of ravage should be filled up, which induced him to make the representations that he did. Now he is not satisfied; he wants to know why another fellow did not take the necessary steps rather than the fellow who is doing it.
I do not know that I ought to go any further, because this is not the time for a debate upon the commercial marine of Canada. I frankly acknowledge that it is a fair subject for discussion whether the building of ships should be done entirely by British capital in this country to the fullest extent of our capacity to assist in that building, or whether we ought as a Government to be building ourselves and consequently to be making up gradually a commercial marine for Canada, having regard to our future needs. That, I say, is a fair subject for discussion, and probably there would not be very much difference of opinion between us on the principle itself. But the member for Pictou acknowledged that there were some difficulties; that ways and means have an important bearing on the matter. The member for Guysborough (Mr. Sinclair), however, was as light as air. I mean in this sense, that there did not seem to be any responsibility from above resting upon him when he stood up and said in a light and airy way that the Government ought to build 200 ships.
Well, Canada is doing a great deal. She is lavishing a vast amount of money, as well as her blood, upon the operations connected with this war. It is impossible for this country to do everything. Two hundred wooden ships of 4,000 tons each would cost from $60,000,000 to $70,000,000; and if they were steel ships they would cost nearly $150,000,000. It is a question whether the best thing is not being done-British capital building the ships for British commerce, and Canada devoting her energies to other kinds of work-costly enough, heaven knows, but borne cheerfully by the people.
I want to caution the House. Maybe hon. gentlemen do not need it; some of them are older than I am, and some are younger. But there is a disposition on the part of hon. gentlemen in this House to cite things that are not done as having been done, and
tSlr George Foster.!
things that are simply rumoured in the papers as being matured decisions of Governments. My hon. friend spoke of the United States having made up its mind to build 1,000 wooden ships. I am not aware that the United States has made up its mind to build 1,000 wooden ships. I know that reams of paper have been given to the dissemination of that idea in the American newspapers, but my latest information is that no decision has been arrived at as to the number of wooden ships that shall be built. My hon. friend thought that there would be no difficulty in our building steel ships. Let me tell him this: for the ships which are being built in Canada to be delivered in 1917, sufficient steel plate has been secured or is in store. For vessels which are to be delivered in 1918, most of the steel plate that is necessary is under contract, and, it is hoped, will be delivered. But you cannot go to the United States to-day -the only place where you can get plates for steel ship building-and make a contract for delivery within a year's time at even the enormous prices which they are charging. Steel plates for shipbuilding could be bought in normal times at 2| cents and 3 cents a pound, whereas to-day they cannot be got at less than 9 cents and even 10 cents a pound. But recollect this: whereas heretofore we have been able to place orders for steel plates in the United States and get deliveries gradually at the increased prices, to-day the United States is commencing to build up the machinery of a mighty offensive effort against the common enemy of us all, and her steel producing activities will be tried to their very utmost in order to meet the necessary demands. It is not and it will not be an easy thing to get steel plate for shipbuilding purposes.
I think one of the members of the House intimated that we might now divert our efforts from munition work to the building of ships. I would not endorse that idea at all. We are all thankful that British activity, organization, scientific skill, and method have increased the small proportions of explosives that were made and the small supplies of guns that were possibilities during the first period of the war, until to-day in explosives and in heavy guns Great Britain is well supplied. Great Britain, however, has Allies and these Allies must also be well supplied if the war is to be carried on to a successful conclusion. Guns wear out and explosives are shot away by the million dollars' worth every day that this war lasts, and the same gigantic, scientifically constructed organi-

zation "which, working with a will, has brought about the splendid condition -as regards explosives and heavy artillery that Great Britain, fortunately for herse'lf, is in to-day must keep vigorously at work on the same scale because of the wastage that takes place and the necessity of constantly implementing what is used. Therefore, I could not say that the war would go on just as well if Canada stopped the making of munitions and turned her attention to the building of wooden ships. The situation would be fraught with peril if we were to shut the doors of our munition factories and were to turn our attention instead to the construction of wooden ships which could be of little service for five, six, or even seven months. I do not think we could justify such a step for a single moment.
Let us not get into a panic in regard to the submarine menace. The submarine is an awful, piratical, destructive engine of war; it has done immense damage; it is doing immense damage now, and it will do immense damage during the whole course of the war, hut the British fleet, with the experience and devotion of its leaders and its personnel, in conjunction with that magnificent fishermen's fleet, 100,000 strong in men whose daily occupation before the waT was the sweeping of the seas for the harvest to lbe garnered therefrom, who have given their services to the Government with a courage, a discipline and a coolness unequalled by the trained men on the battleships, has swept those dangerous seas for the safety of the commerce of the whole world. That fishermen's fleet has swept those dangerous seas and is sweeping them every hour and every day with sometimes not a hair's breadth between those gallant fishermen and sudden and certain destruction. It is that less splendid but not less serviceable part of the British naval work- the fishermen's mine sweeping and trawling work-that, added to the British navy, and backed up and supported by newer methods of fighting submarines which are every day coming to the front has done and will continue to do that important work that make us feel that although there is tremendous peril and great destruction of life and of property still ahead of us, it is not sufficient to break the confidence of the Allies and of the British Empire, as a part of the Allies, in 'the coming final real victory for which we are all working.	[DOT]

I understood the minister to say that British capital is now available for the construction of Canadian ships in Canadian yards. This is news to some of us as it has not been made public before and it is very important news. Will the minister, therefore, be kind enough to tell us on what terms a builder can secure British capital?

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: A builder does not personally secure British capital, but if he makes a bona fide offer and shows that he has the financial capacity, equipment, and the labour to build those vessels, he will be given a contract up to the extent of his capacity.
I understood the minister to state further that a guarantee would be given that no loss would occur to the parties undertaking the building of ships.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: I stand by what I said. That will be the case.
Does the Imperial Munitions Board give that guarantee?

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext:
The Imperial
Munitions Board acting for the British Government.
It is curious that they did not give that information to the public.
Mr. Speaker, unless any other hon. gentleman desires to speak, I will now proceed to close the debate.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
If any other
hon. member wishes to speak on this subject, he must do so before the hon. member for Pictou speaks again.

Mr. Speaker, my right hon. friend, desiring to evade the question, has indulged in that warmth of speech of which he is such an admirable master. As my right hon. friend has reproached me for introducing this subject in the way in which I did, I may say that I was well within the rules and absolutely justified in bringing this question before the House; and if I were not justified, then no other matter can be conceived that can be brought before the House on the consideration of a motion that . the House do now adjourn. This is a most important question for the consideration of Parliament; it is one that was discussed in the Imperial Parliament on Tuesday of this week when there were none of these suggestions or whisperings or insinuations that you must not say this or that or the German Kaiser will hear what you say on the floor of the Imperial

Parliament. Instead of that, the members were told: You are the free representatives of Great Britain discussing this, the greatest menace of the war. Yet my right hon. friend suggests here to-day the bugaboo that we, the representatives of a free people in this country, must not look the situation in the face and must not ask this Government whether they are realizing the menace that the Imperial Government have realized; we are' told we must not speak except with bated breath. When my right hon. friend indulges in statements of that kind by way of pretext, I reject any such suggestion. This matter is one of the greatest importance before Great Britain or any of her Allies. It has been discussed in their Parliaments; it forms the common subject of discussion in-the press of the United States. The President of the United States, the Secretary of State, and the Secretary of the Interior deal publicly with this question and the part they are going to play in order to meet and overcome this great menace; but when we come to this Canadian Government, >it clothes itself iwith holiness and declares that nobody must venture to suggest that with its omniscience it can do wrong, and that no one in this free country muet venture to suggest that it should do or not do anything. That is the atitude of my right hon. friend. If he fancies that the people of this free country, the red-blooded men of Canada, are going to submit to that kind of dictatorial Kaiser-ism, he is making a great mistake. Either there is a menace ox there is not one; and if there is, what is this Government doing to deal with it? I said nothing with regard to the situation in the Maritime Provinces or anything else that required any homilies from my right hon. friend. He has told us that the British Navy has been wonderfully successful in giving us protection and in transporting our men and supplies across the ocean; I cordially agree. But here was a new menace. The British Admiralty admitted in the House of Commons the gravity of the situation. Yet in the House of Commons here nobody must say anything about it. If we do, we are helping the Germans! Such ridiculous absurdities can hardly stand the light of day in this twentieth century in our free Parliament. What does my hon. friend say that he is doing about this menace? He wound up with a peroration paying a glowing tribute to the British Navy which we all admire; but although the United States are spending one billion dollars to build 
up a merchant marine the minister says that Canada should not do anything. He says that the Imperial Munition Board is building ships in this country with British money, to which the Canadian Government are contributing; everything that is proper to be done is being done; it is treasonable to ask any questions about it; that is what my hon. friend said.

What about the overseas Minister of Militia?
Mr- MACDONALD: Yes, the great overseas Minister of Militia, who is so much admired by the ex-Minister of Militia, the man on whom Canada pins her faith. But I will not turn aside to discuss that gentleman's capacity and Tecord, as we shall probably have an opportunity at some other time except to say that everybody who has been in England knows how little fit he is to guide the destinies of Canada's overseas forces- My hon. friend says that the Munitions Board are building wooden ships in Canada with British money, to which the Canadian Government is contributing, and that we must not ask anything more about the matter. We are not going to build ships. I asked the Minister of Finance the other day what this Government waS doing in the way of building ships, and he said: "The matter is under consideration." Now we have the statement of the Minister of Trade and Commerce that even if the matter was under consideration, nothing is going to be done about it, because the Imperial Munitions Board are building wooden ships. My hon. friend from Guysborough tried to get some information, but he was no more successful than I. The minister tells us Canadian money is being given the Imperial Munitions Board, a body that is not responsible to the Canadian people, and that the Board is going to build ships for somebody. We cannot tell you anything more than that, he says. We must take it for granted that these things are being done. I say that we will have to have a full statement from my hon. friend at some later date as to just what the Imperial Munitions Board are undertaking to do, what ships they are building, and where they are being built. My hon. friend intimates to the House that the Government, as a government, do not propose to insist upon the construction of either steel or wooden ships in this country. The Government of the greatest overseas dominion of this Empire, living adjacent as we do to our great Anglo-Saxon neighbour, are going to do nothing as a government in the way

of building ships. The United States realized the necessity of filling up the gaps created in the merchant marine and in the navies by the German submarines, and that country is doing splendidly, but this Government does not propose to do anything. We ajre going to let the British Government do it all through the Imperial Munitions Board. We are not going to give one dollar, although vessels of Canadian registration, flying the Canadian flag, and transporting Canadian goods, are being sunk week after week. Our whole merchant marine may be obliterated before the war is over, and yet the Minister of Trade and Commerce of the greatest dominion in the Empire is responsible for the statement that Canada will not do a single thing or give a single dollar towards shipbuilding.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: The Minister of Trade and Commerce is not responsible for any such statement, for he never made any such statement, and he is not at all responsible for any inferences that my hon. friend chooses to draw.
What is the Government doing?

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: Hansard will give you exactly what I said. I generally am able to make my meaning plain. If my hon. friend will see what I said in Hansard to-morrow, and will put that side by side with what he has just said, if he is fair, he will be crying " peccavi " to-morrow afternoon.

If my hon. friend has made any statement indicating that the Government are contributing a dollar by way of bonus, or subvention, or in any other way towards the construction of ships in this country then I am sorry, for I must have misunderstood him. If he has indicated that this Government, as a government, is providing for the construction of ships in Canada, I did not so understand him, and if he did make any statements of that kind I pause for a moment to see if he will repeat them.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext:
I do not know whether or not I can succeed in enlightening my hon. friend. I made a statement with regard to certain things that were being done. I did not make any statement as to what the Canadian Government proposes to do in the future with reference to shipbuilding. I am not called upon to make any such statement. There will be a time when the Government will make known what it proposes to do imthat regard. If I
did not say in my remarks that the Canadian Government was expending its own money in the construction of a number of these vessels, then I probably did not go as far as I should have done-but, that is the case.
Where are they being constructed?

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext:
In Canada, at
different shipyards.
Have contracts been let?

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: Contracts have been given, and some of the vessels will be ready to take the water in June.
Where are these vessels being built?
Is there anything else you want to know?

If my hon. friend
thinks that this free Parliament is run by the decrees of an internal body, well, he may be Tory enough to believe it. The Minister of Trade and Commerce knows that this Parliament has a right to know whether contracts have been let for these vessels. He is too old a parliamentarian not to know that.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext:
Certainly this
Parliament has a right to know, and if my hon. friend wishes to know he will get his information. I am not quite sure-and here again I shall offend the democratic susceptibilities of my hon. friend-when he will get exact information as to the number of patrol vessels and mine sweepers that are being constructed by the Dominion of Canada at the present time. I am not sure that he will get that information; I am not sure that it is wise that he should.

We have succeeded in getting some information at all events, but I would say to my hon. friend, if it is possible for the British Government and the Government of the United States to give to the people who supply the funds to 'enable them to administer the affairs of the country, information such as has been given to them in this regard, I see no reason why my hon. friend should not give *similar information to this House.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext:
Let my hon.
friend be fair. Will he point out any particular time within the last two years when either in the United States or in Great Britain the men who have charge of this mat-

ter of 'building vessels for the purpose of meeting the enemy's warships, either under the sea or on the sea, have detailed the places at which they were -being built, the kind of vessels which were being built, or the number? I was in England last summer and by the courtesy of the British [DOT]Government I had the opportunity with others who were with me to see the inside of the building -and operating work which was going ,on there, to meet the German peril both undersea and overhead. I was shown these things under the seal of -secrecy, and not a note could I take, not a note did I take, during all that time. I want my hon. -friend to point out where, either -in the United States or in Great Britain, this particular information has been given.

My right hon. friend (Sir George Foster) knows very well that, while in the Government circles these things are regarded as matters of secrecy, in the shipyards of the country the number and character of vessels under construction is a matter of common knowledge, both in Great Britain and the United States. He knows that if he will turn to the English Hansard he will find there statements given in regard to the shipbuilding that is going on. He will find that, repeatedly, Lloyd George himself has made statements as to the number of vessels of various classes under construction and their tonnage. But all we have been able to extract from the right hon. gentleman (Sir George Foster) is that some mine-sweepers are being built. But he will not permit me to say, and I hope he will take no exception to my way of saying it, that on the question of assisting toward making good the deficiencies in our merchant marine, caused by the action of the enemy, we are left to infer that the Government are doing nothing.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: My hon. friend will allow me to be definite. He has stated that both in the United States, in the Congress or outside of it, and in Great Britain, in their Parliament or outside of it, those in authority have repeatedly given information as to the. war vessels under construction, their kinds and dimension and where they were being built. Will he substantiate that by something more than a general statement? Will he show me his authority?
I shall be glad to give it at the proper time-
Oh, oh.
The right hon. gentleman comes to us-

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: I will give my hon. friend any time he likes, if he will only do it.

I am glad the right hon. gentleman accepts the suggestion. I am sure he appreciates the fact that this Government, naturally and properly, should accept it under the circumstances. He has very promptly drawn the discussion away from the main subject to a side issue. He has evaded the substantial question, whether this Government proposes to do anything to assist in the construction of merchant vessels in this country to fly the Canadian flag and to fill the vacancies which take place in our merchant marine day by day. The policy of the Government under consideration a week ago is still under consideration, and nothing is done. He utterly misapprehends my motive in bringing this matter to the attention of the House. I have urged, as it was my right to do, and as has been urged in England and elsewhere, the necessity of the Government dealing with these matters in some definite way. So far as our merchant marine is concerned, we are left to understand that nothing will be done. We are told that arrangements are being made in some other way. But so far as the great question which has been dealt with by both the British government and the United States government, where they faced' the issue openly and fairly, and made their announcement as to what they were going to do, the right hon. gentleman evades the question. We have no policy of this Government in regard to assisting the construction of merchant vessels in Canada, either by the Government themselves or by subvention or other assistance. We are not told that the Government is grappling with that phase of the question or undertaking to deal with it in any way.
As it is six o'clock, Mr. Speaker, and as I cannot be here when the House resumes, I ask leave to withdraw my motion.
Motion withdrawn.

On the Orders of the Day:

Mr. Speaker, I would like to get a little infor-

mation if possible, from my hon. friend who is leading the House (Sir George Foster). I have the following telegram from Winnipeg :
Try and get something definite on import duty on wheat and wheat products under new proposed tax in the United States. Great uneasiness here owing to large cargoes lying over there which were either released from bond or have been left over ever since supposedly free wheat.
I presume the information that is wanted is as to the position of wheat cargoes that were released from bond over there, but probably not disposed of. I am not sure of that but that is what it appears to be. In the meantime there is a duty of 10 per cent on wheat going into the United States as a war duty and I presume they desire to know if the Government has any information as to whether that duty would cover cargoes of wheat which have been released from bond and not disposed of.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: The Bill in reference to which my hon. friend (Mr. Turriff) speaks is only at present a Bill which has been reported from the committee to the House. There has been as yet, in so far as I know, no discussion of it in the House and no one knows how that Bill will come out of the House. My hon. friend has just as much information as I have, or as can be got, until the Bill is acted upon and becomes law in one form or another.
It is not law at the present time?

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: No.

speechtext: On the Orders of the Day:

I deside to draw attention to a statement appearing in Hansard on February 7. Hansard says:
Sir ROBERT BORDEN laid on the table of the House a report by Colonel Bruce on the Canadian Army Medical Service.
He said: This is the only copy that is available on this side of the ocean at the present moment. I have, however, decided that it had better be laid on the table of the House, as further copies are coming in the immediate future. I should explain that it is marked "confidential, for official use only." Under ordinary conditions, I should think it ought not to be brought down ; but it would appear that it has been made public, wholly or partially, through the press, I do not know in what way. Further, it seems to me that to avoid any misconception and understanding which might arise, if it was not brought down and laid upon the table of the House, It is better to take that
course than to refuse to lay upon the Table a document which was intended only for confidential official use in the first instance.
Will it be printed during the recess ?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
It is being printed now, I understand. Some forty copies, I think, are coming from England by mail. These will be available, and we will have further copies printed if necessary.
I am also laying upon the table of the House the report of the Board of Inquiry of whicli Sir William Babtie was chairman. This report deals with practically the same matter as the report I have already laid upon the table of the House, and it is proper that if the one report is placed before the House and the country, the other report should also be made public.
Understanding from the statement made to the House on February 7 that it was the intention of the Government that this report should be printed for the information of the public, I applied at the distribution office yesterday for copies of this report and was informed that they were not available for distribution and that the report was not being printed. I would like to ask the Government if that is the position of affairs?

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: Whether the report is being printed here or not I do not know, but 'we have a number of copies which have come over, as intimated, from England, and my hon. friend can be served with a copy on application to the clerk.

I may say in connection with this matter that when the report was first laid on the Table I got a copy from the clerk in charge and was getting some extracts from it for later use when the King's Printer was very anxious to get it and sent for it. He told me that there was quite a number being printed and that there would be no trouble in getting all the copies we wanted.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: I will make inquiry as to whether it is being printed and how far it has got on. There is no objection to its being printed, if it is necessary.

In this connection, I wish to draw attention to a statement which appeared in the press that Dr. Bruce made a defence, if I would understand it in that way, or a reply, to the Babtie report which was placed by him in the hands, of the Minister of Militia. I would ask if it is the intention of the Government to make public this reply or report of Dr. Bruce.
1.344

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: I will make inquiry in reference to that and let my hon. friend know.
