speakerposition: subtopic
speechtext:
['Mr. Viviani, in the person of her distinguished visitor, Canada today hails
[Sir Wilfrid Laurier.i
the official representative of France, France at all times wonderful, but who during the last three years has held and is now holding ever increasingly the world in amazement; France, of whom you have spoken with such eloquence; France, united in a sacred union, which has put an end to all feuds, differences or shades of opinion, everything that disunited her sons; and which has placed her where she stands to-day, the champion,, not only of her own freedom, but of the liberties of the world.
We greet you as the representative of France, and that greeting 'it is particularly pleasing to me to express in the French language, of which you have just spoken with such eloquence, a language which has the limpidity of a stream and the resistance of metal, which our forefathers have 'brought with them from the country of your ancestors and kept as their most, sacred heritage.
You Visited the United States, accompanied by that illustrious general. . . .
(Long applause).
by that illustrious general who at the beginning of the war had been entrusted with the destinies of France, and who was successful in 'breaking the German offensive, and destroying for ever the enemy's plans for establishing German supremacy. You have visited all the great cities, and everywhere you have, been greeted with a spontaneity, an outburst, an enthusiasm that must have sometimes astonished you and always exceeded your hopes.
You now cross from one country to another, from the land of the United States to the land of Canada, a British soil. Many are the historic ties that bind you to the United States; but stronger are those that unite you to Canada's soil; because if you have met everywhere in the United States the feeling of admiration which the mere name of France evokes here, on this British soil, you will find not only admiration, but along with our sympathy you will find national pride; you will meet two million citizens of French descent who have kept alive the cult of France, a cult, that honours France, for inspiring it, Canada for fostering it, and England for respecting it.
But I hasten to add that, if we keep up the pride of our origin, we are equally proud of our allegiance. I say our allegiance; the word has somewhat fallen into disuse in France, but it was brought from France, into England by the Normans and brought from England into Canada. We are proud of our allegiance, because wherever rights exist duties are born. We enjoy the rights of our origin, we have the duties of our allegiance, and for both we have an equal respect.

Mr. Viviani, your stay amongst us is too brief; you will soon depart; let me tell you that you leave 'behind a souvenir never to be blotted out of our memory, and that whatever happens, we shall remain true to the cause we are fighting for. We shall persevere until final victory, be that victory at hand, as we hope, or be it distant, as may *be; we are in the struggle to the end. And we have no doubt of a victorious outcome, because we, in Canada, as you, in France, have the common resolve never to lay down arms until right and justice, have again taken their place under the sun.
The DEPUTY SPEAKER [DOT]: Sir George Foster moves, seconded by Sir Wilfrid Laurier:
That the admirable and eloquent speech just delivered by M. Viviani be inserted .in the Official Report of the Debates of this House, and that it form a part o-f the permanent record of this Parliament.
Motion agreed to by a standing vote.
Hon. Sir GEORGE FOSTER moved the adjournment of the House.
He said: Before the adjournment, I beg to say that if the ladies and gentlemen present will be kind enough to walk in at the right of Mr. Speaker, and out at his left, M. Viviani will add to the gracious debt under which he has already placed us by giving them a personal greeting.
The audience then sang La Marseillaise and God Save the King, and in response to the call of the Deputy Speaker cheered " Vive la France."
Motion agreed to and House adjourned at 1.20 p.m.
Monday, May 14, 1917.']

speakeroldname: Hon. W. J. ROCHE (Minister of the Interior) :
speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: This is to pay the salaries of all the outside staff numbering 447, the same number as last year. This includes the salaries of the staffs of all our land agencies in the West, timber inspectors, homestead inspectors, inspectors of land agencies, ranches, and sub-agencies.

I wish to repeat the criticism I made last year that, in my humble judgment, the condition of the business of the department of the Interior in the West does not warrant a large expenditure of this kind. It is being urged upon the country that there should be saving in all lines on account of the heavy drain on the resources of the country because of the war.
I desire to take the responsibility of saying here and now that in my judgment-and I speak as one having some knowledge of the subject-this is an absolutely unwarrantedly large expenditure at this time and under these circumstances, and that this item should not be as large as it is.

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: My hon. friend's criticism, I presume, refers to the expenditures of the Interior Department generally. This particular item, of course, is for the Outside Service.
I refer particularly to this item.

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: That would mean that the hon. gentleman thinks that out staff is over manned?

Absolutely over manned.
Mr, ROCHE:	My information is quite
the contrary. We have 160 of those men who are doing duty at the front. The places of many of these we have not filled, in fact that has only been done where it was absolutely essential to do so. These men are drawing an average of about $1,000 apiece, which is a small salary, comparatively speaking, taking the whole outside service, in this period of 'high cost of living. Our land offices have been extremely busy in connection with the extra work entailed [Mr. Oliver.!
by the seed grain advancement. We have been using our land office staff, our homestead inspectors, etc., during the winter months, and they have been kept very busy. In fact in certain classes out there it is almost impossible to secure help at the present salaries, particularly in the case of clerical help and stenographers. Some of our staff are leaving because of the low salaries. I am inundated with applications for increased salaries from the outside staff, because they are underpaid. There are many in the Inside Service at Ottawa drawing $700 to $900 arid the hon. gentleman will realize, I am sure, as he is a western man, that the cost of living there is at least as high as it is in Ottawa. It is considered essential ,to introduce legislation at this .session to increase the salaries of the lower grades of the Inside Service, and I was seriously considering doing the same thing in connection with the outside service, applying the increase on the same basis to those getting $60, $65 and $75 per month. I do not think it is possible to cut down our staff at the present time. They have been very busy, and I disagree with the hon. gentleman in his statement that we should dispense with their services, in view of the fact that fully 160 of them have enlisted and gone to the front.

Does the minister mean to say that there are 160 of the employees of the Interior Department who are at the front and are drawing their salaries from the Interior Department as well as their military pay, and rendering no service to the Interior Department?

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: I do not say that. I say there are about 160 who have enlisted from the outside service. Many of those are overseas. Some of them enlisted prior to the Order in Council which provided for the pay of the civil salary less military salary. That is, they are drawing full salary. Those who enlisted prior to November 1, 1915, are drawing their full civil service salary, and those who enlisted since then have their military pay deducted from their civil pay. In some instances we have had to replace those men, but we have been trying to avoid filling their places unless'it was absolutely essential to do so.

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext:
There is a reduction of
some 530,000 here below the Estimates last year.
Surveys, $776,300.

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext:
There is a reduction of
$200,000 from the Estimate of last year.

Where are these surveys
being made principally?

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext:
Surveys of base lines and
initial meridians, three parties; sub-division surveys, sixteen parties; miscellaneous subdivision surveys in Manitoba, Saskatchewan and Alberta, one party; sub-division surveys in the railway belt of British Columbia, five parties; inspection surveys, six inspectors and one party for general business; retracement surveys in Manitoba, Alberta and Saskatchewan, two parties; retracement surveys of old initial meridians and base lines, one party; miscellaneous surveys 'by travelling parties, four parties; stadia surveys of lakes in western provinces, said to have dried up, eleven parties; survey of the Alberta and British Columbia boundary (one-third share), two parties; Yukon surveys. That is practically the subdivision of the work for the ensuing year.

In regard to this survey
Estimate, the minister did not say just in what part of the country these surveys were being made. I shall not press that point. I wish to point out that the men employed on these survey parties are of necessity of the identical quality of physique, age and other requirements that make for eligibility for military service, and I cannot think that the Government is well advised in pushing the surveys unless those surveys are urgently required at such a time w'hen it must Ibe done at such cost in the employment of men who, as I have said, by their age and physique, are the men who are most eligible for military service.
If we are looking for more men for military service, we might very well restrict our endeavours in the matter of pushing surveys, particularly at a time when there is no very great pressure of settlement in any direction. The need for men who are physically fit for military service is, of course, great, and the men who are employed on the surveys are necessarily of that class. They cannot be serving in France and working on the surveys at the same time, and, looking at it from that standpoint alone, I submit that the Government are not well advised in pressing the surveys as strongly as they are doing just now'.

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: I myself was of the opinion that it was not necessary to push the surveys as rapidly as heretofore, taking into consideration the war conditions. For that reason, during the past year, we cut down our expenditure by $200,000, and this year we are estimating an expenditure of $200,000 less than last year. There is, therefore, really a very great reduction in the expenditure. As for those who go out on the survey parties, instructions have been issued that whenever possible, returned soldiers be employed for that purpose. The Surveyor-General has pointed out to me the difficulty in getting many returned soldiers who are able to endure the hardships of the survey, but they are to be given the preference in every instance.
Is the amount that is being asked for equal to the amount expended last year?

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: Practically what was expended last year.

I have observed a good deal of discussion in the press about the amount of land available for returned soldiers; it has been questioned whether we have very much land suitable for that

purpose in the title of the country. I am quite sure that it would he interesting if the minister could tell us how many acres of arable land in the northwest and the prairie provinces are in the hands of the Government and available for homesteading.

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: Much the same information was asked for by the right hon. leader of the Opposition when I explained the soldiers' settlement plan as laid down in the resolution which I brought before the House, and I promised to have a map here when the resolution is again under consideration, showing the location of lands, within ten, fifteen or twenty miles of a railway, which are suitable for agriculture. A statement has been prepared as to the amount; I did not bring it with me to-night, but I promised to give the information as fully ias possible when the soldiers' settlement resolution is again before the House.
What parties will be working in the Peace River country, and in what localities?

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: I do not think I have the detailed information here.

In a time like the present this seems to be an enormous sum of money to expend on the surveying of land which is not being settled. Putting it at $1,500 a man, which would probably be the maximum, you have 500 men employed in surveying western lands during the year. But during at least half the year these men could not be employed in surveying lands; therefore, you have an army of 1,000 men employed in surveying lands in western Canada during six months of the year. It seems a large amount of money to he expended-I was going to say thrown away, but I assume that these surveys may be of value some time in the future. To the man living in the eastern portion of Canada, however, the question arises why it should be necessary to expend this large amount of money when the public debt is mounting up by $200,000,000 or $300,000,000 a year. I think the minister ought to take us into his confidence and tell us how many parties and how many men are being employed and what they are doing.

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: The hon. gentleman is rather extravagant in his assertions when he says that we have 1,000 men employed on this work during the year. He must remember that surveyors are technical men, and draw a fairly good salary, particularly when out in the field.

But many cooks and
labouring men are employed in this work who do not draw big salaries.

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: The hon. gentleman knows, too, that aside from the expenditure for salaries, the outfit for work of this kind costs a considerable amount. There is a man in charge of each survey party; there is an assistant, and sometimes a second assistant. There are the chain men, so many in each party-ten men in one party, twelve in another. They have to go into the wilds; they have to be provisioned, and transportation costs something. We exercised due economy in cutting down the expenditure of last year by $200,000, and, as I have said, we mean to cut down the present appropriation by $200,000. It is essential that that part of the country particularly be opened up. The hon. member suggests that not many people are going in there. Well, I have word from the northern part of Alberta a short time ago that immigrants are going in there very rapidly from the United States. Some of them are going away disappointed because the lands are not at their disposal. I did not throw open any large blocks of land, pending the legislation with respect to land for returned soldiers, as it was my intention, wherever possible, to keep the lands that were close to transportation facilities for the returned soldiers. I have given information as to the number of parties that will be sent out, but I have not detailed information as to the parties going into any particular section.
How many parties did the minister say were going out?

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext:
In the surveys of base lines and initial meridians, two parties. Some of these parties consist of 8, 10 or 12 men. On subdivision surveys, 16 parties. A lot of our survey work is subdivision surveys, that is subdividing the townships. There are five parties working in subdivision surveys in the railway belt. As the work of those parties that are out has to be inspected, we have inspection surveys, and there are six inspectors and one party for general business. We have two parties engaged in retracement surveys in the wsetem provinces, and one party doing retracement survey work of the old initial meridians and base lines. There are four parties for miscellaneous surveys and eleven parties for stadia surveys of lakes reported to have dried up in the western provinces. Many

of the homesteaders who, when they secured patents for their lands had a certain quantity of water on them, have since found that the water has dried up and they apply to have the dried-up area added to their homesteads. This requires surveying and we had eleven parties out for that purpose. Then there are two parties engaged in surveys of the British Columbia-Alberta boundary line. That is done by the Governments of the two provinces and the Dominion Government, each bearing their share of the expense. There are three parties engaged in levelling. There are other expenditures in connection with the manufacture and storage of iron posts and bench marks, printing and stationery, lithographers' and printers' wages, freight, express and telegraph charges, purchase of instruments and canvas boats foT use on the surveys. Then there are surveys unprovided for which may be urgently required during the season, carpenter for surveys laboratory and special surveys division. In the Outside service there are thirty-four office employees at $1.50 per day. All these expenses amount, in the aggregate, to a very large sum. I do not know exactly the number of those who will be engaged in survey work; I simply know the number of parties that will be engaged, and as the number of men employed on each party differs considerably, I cannot give the details.

The minister has answered the whole criticism. I took down rough notes of what he said, and, as I figure it out, there are 24 or 25 parties who are going over old work, retracing old lines, seeing how much water has receded and how much land can he reclaimed. The minister has in his employ 250 men whose salaries probably amount to $250,000, which i3 an absolutely unnecessary expense. The people in the western provinces can do just as we do in the eastern portion of Canada, where if two neighbours cannot agree upon their lines, they fight the matter out in the courts; they look after their surveys and pay their own bills. It is just as I thought; the minister, in my judgment, has answered the whole criticism- Here we have half a million dollars being thrown away.

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: The hon. member is comparing the little province of New Brunswick with the western provinces where we own land.

The province of New
Brunswick will compare favourably with the western provinces, and if the minister
will follow out in the western country the conditions that prevail in New Brunswick, he will do a great deal better than he is doing. The province of New Brunswick has done well in many ways.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext:
That remark
holds for the late Government.

Might I ask the minister to revert to the first item, " Salaries of the Outside Service?" I wish to ask a question in regard to a gentleman whose name was mentioned here last year or the year before. I refer to the gentleman who holds the position, of superintendent of Jasper park and who, I believe, was appointed a colonel in the overseas forces. I wish to ask if this gentleman is still drawing salary as superintendent of Jasper park and if he is still drawing pay as a colonel in the overseas forces-

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: I can answer for my own department; I cannot answer for the Militia Department. He is not on the paylist of the Interior Department.
Since what time has he ceased to be on that .pay-list?

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext:
A short time-I do not
know just how long after he returned from across the ocean, he was struck off the list. I may say that the request did not have to come from the head of the department. He asked to have his name struck off.

Is that policy being
carried out generally throughout the department, of returned officers being struck off the Civil Service pay-list?

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: If they have a military duty assigned to them, of course they will be kept on the pay-list, but if they have nothing of a military character to do, they have either to return to their civil duties or be struck off the list.

In the case I had in view, the officer, on returning from the front, had military work assigned to him in the way of instructional work during the past summer; but under the present state of recruiting, there is not very much of that sort of work going on at the present time, and I understand he is still drawing military pay as well as civil Bay- I understand the minister made it a policy that if a man returned from the front he ceased to draw civil pay even if he was on military duty in his country.

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: If we receive word from the military authorities that a man's services are absolutely necessary for the Militia Department, we keep him on the pay list. We do not strike him off the pay list if we get that assurance from the military authorities; we treat him just as we treat a soldier in Canada who has not yet proceeded overseas.

The difference in the case of the soldier in Canada is that he is just drawing from his department the difference in pay between his civil and his military pay, whereas, all soldiers enlisted prior to the 1st of November, 1915, are drawing full civil pay as well as full military pay. Does the minister intend to carry out that policy in its entirety of paying in full a soldier who enlisted prior to the 1st of November, 1915, whether he requires the money or not?

I am given to understand that we have very few in our department who are drawing full pay; that is, very few who have returned who had enlisted prior to the 1st of November, 1915, but in each instance we must get an assurance from the military authorities that a man's services are required by the Militia Department before we retain him on the pay roll of our department.

In regard to the late superintendent of Jasper park, has the minister not received an assurance from the military authorities that the gentleman is in military employment now? I understood the minister to say that he had no knowledge of the facts.	_

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: I did not say that I had no knowledge; I said that Colonel Maynard Rogers, who is the gentleman I presume the hon. member refers to-
Yes.

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: -was struck off the pay roll at his own request. My hon. friend would not ask me to keep that gentleman on the pay roll against his desire.

Certainly not. That much may be counted as merit to the Minister of the Interior, and if he would follow that policy from now on, he would acquire more merit in the eyes of the taxpayers of Canada. Has a permanent superintendent of Jasper park been appointed?

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext:
A temporary appointment has been made. The name of the appointee has escaped me for a moment, but the

gentleman whom the hon. member has in mind has been appointed temporarily during Colonel Maynard Rogers' absence. Just the same as in the case of all civil servants who enlist, we make temporary appointments to fill their places. We are merely making a temporary appointment.
As Colonel Maynard Rogers' connection with the department has ceased, it would be in order, I presume, for a permanent appointment to be made.

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: Colonel Rogers is still in the employ of the Militia Department.

I understood the minister to say that when he was satisfied the Militia Department were continuing in their employ an official of the Interior Department who, under the terms of enlistment, was entitled to full salary in both departments, he was continued in both services. In the case of the superintendent of Jasper Park, although he is in military employ, his civil service has ceased. What I am asking is whether a permanent appointment is to be made. I am not asking out of mere curiosity. Summer is now approaching, and I am sure the minister will agree that it is desirable that whoever is to be permanently in charge of the park should be appointed now. If the gentleman who has been in charge for the last two years is to be appointed permanently it would be entirely in order for the appointment to be mads now, and he would then be able to carry out his ideas in regard to the development of the park. I do not think it is well for the park, if the minister will pardon me for saying so, to be without a permanent superintendent.

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext:
When Colonel Rogers is released from his military duties he will be without a position, and it would appear to me to be a breach of faith to make a permanent appointment in his absence on military duty. He has been overseas and is now retained in the service of the Militia Department. He asked to be taken off the pqy-list of the Interior Department, and when he went away we appointed Mr. Driscoll temporarily. He is from the hon. gentleman's own city of Edmonton, and has been acting superintendent of the park for two or three years. Mr. Driscoll quite understands that he was appointed temporarily. I am informed that he has done excellent work, and there is no uncertainty about following out development work as my hon. friend seems to

think. Mr. Driscoll is an excellent officer, and i3 doing very good work, and I am snre he will continue to do so until the time comes when Colonel Rogers will be released from his military position and resume his duties.

I am very, very sorry that it is not possible to place the ip.ark under permanent administration. If it is the intention to reappoint Colonel Rogers I think he should resume his civil duties without delay. I do not wish to be understood as offering any objection to Colonel Rogers' resuming his duties as superintendent of Jasper Park, but I want to urge that there should not be the uncertainty that has prevailed in regard to the administration of the park during the last couple of years. It should be thoroughly understood who is to be permanently in charge, so that he may develop the park along his own lines. The present temporary superintendent is, I bekeve, entirely satisfactory, but he certainly is handicapped in not having the assurance of being able to carry out any policy he may undertake. I think, in fairness to the development of the park, the minister should decide who is to be permanently in charge, and get him established there now, so that he can proceed to develop the park along his own lines.
Protection of timber in Manitoba, Saskatchewan, Aiberta, the N.W.T., and the Kailway Belt in B.C., tree culture in (Manitoba, Saskatchewan, Alberta, and inspection and management of forest reserves, $650,000.

I think this is another
case where the minister might have made a saving. I will not press the matter further than to emphasize what I have already said, that I consider this and other items in the Estimates entirely extravagant under present conditions. Would the minister tell me what is included under "tree culture in Manitoba, Saskatchewan and Alberta"! Is it tree culture on forest reserves or in connection with the Forestry Farm?

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext:
I have the following particulars :	i
Trees are supplied to farmers for planting on prairie farms In the provinces of Manitoba, Saskatchewan and Alberta. The species distributed are mainly Manitoba maple, elm, ash, cottonwood, Russian poplar and willow. Some spruce, tamarack and pine have also been distributed. The reports of the inspectors show that these plantations have a high average of success. There are two nurseries for this purpose. One was established at Indian Head in 1903, and one at Sutherland in 1912. The increased demand from farmers for trees made necessary the increase of accomodation for furnishing the supply. The new nursery is now supplying trees for distribution, and this supply will be largely increased in the next few years as this nursery develops. The number of trees distributed in the last two seasons is as follows:	3,861,000 trees were distributed in
1915 to 3,459 applicants, and 4,460,000 trees were distributed in 1916 to 5,072 applicants. The total number of trees distributed to date is 37,539,105. The number now ready for distribution in the spring of 1917 is 8,881,500.
Hon. gentlemen will see that the demand for the trees is increasing very largely, and I am sure we are all pleased to see that, because trees are beneficial in more ways than one in that prairie country. The new nursery at Sutherland is doing excellent work.
Are these trees for use on private lands?

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: They are distributed gratis to the farmers all through the western provinces, on demand.

Will the minister do
the same for the eastern provinces?

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: These are Dominion lands.
Not after they are homesteaded or purchased.

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext:
In the hon. gentleman's
province the lands and timber are owned by the provincial government, and I presume the provincial governments do similar work to what we are doing for the West.

I think the minister
should draw a distinction between land owned by the province and land owned by the individual. The arable lands will, all be under private ownership very soon. Why should not trees be given free to the other provinces?	.	-

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: These provinces are " treeless."

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: And probably the supply of trees would not be suitable to the other provinces.
What does this branch of the work cost?

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: The amount estimated for this year is $58,000, and the amount for last year was $67,030.
What proportion of the balance of this vote is required for the administration of the forest reserves as compared with the proportion for the protection of timber not included in forest reserves?

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: For forest reserves we have an item of $299,000, and for fire-ranging $193,000. The total for forest reserve, fireranging, and the forest products laboratory is $650,000.

My information is that there is an entirely unreasonable proportion of expenditure on the so-called forest reserves as compared with that for the protection of timbers not included in forest reserves. The Government has been very liberal in including large areas in forest reserves. These areas are forested to 'a certain extent, of course, but in a country that is all forested it seems to be hardly necessary that areas should be specially reserved, especially when they are made a preserve rather for the maintenance of friends of the Government in the guise of protectors of public property than to serve any particularly useful purpose. The forest reserves, in my humble judgment, are unnecessarily large, and there is excessive expenditure in the so-called protective service within those reserves.
' Mr. ROCHE: Of course, an area is first surveyed and temporarily set aside before being included in the forest reserve by legislation. The hon gentleman (Mr. Oliver) knows that there has been great destruction of timber in that country-as has been the case in the East also-by fire. Land that on inspection is ascertained to be not suitable for agriculture is included in the forest reserves and comes under the charge of the officials, part of whose duties is to protect the forest from fire. It would not be right to have homesteaders go upon land from which they could l.ot make a living. The hon. gentleman (Mr. Oliver), as minister, had experience, as I have had, with so-called settlers who have no intention of living on the land after it is cleared, but who simply squat and, when the timber is gone, vacate the holding. Of course, there are some areas included In forest reserves that are timbered lightly or not at all, but these lands are suitable for reforestation and are not suitable for agriculture.
Who is in charge of the Cooking Lake forest reserve?

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: Mr. Bailey.

How many officials are
employed in connection with the Moose Mountain reserve? I was there two months, ago and heard a good many complaints of the amount the officials were charging settlers for firewood.

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext:
The amount charged for
firewood is fixed by regulation, and I do not think more is charged on the Moose Mountain reserve than on any other.

I heard of a couple of

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior

Two permanaent and one
temporary. Mr. White is in charge.
How many officials are employed in the forest reserves altogether?

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior

The number employed in

Does that include the
forest rangers and timber inspectors?

The hon. gentleman has not told me how much he paid the men on Moose Mountain reserve?

The man in charge gets
$100 a month, and the others $75 a month.
How many fire-rangers, inspectors and other protectors of timber are employed on the Swan Hills forest reserve, and how many on the Martin Mountain forest reserve?

Would the minister say why the salaries for part of the outside service are put under the heading of "Salaries of the Outside Service $465,000 '' and a lot more of the salaries put in the item we are now discussing under " Protection of Timber in (Manitoba?" They are all under

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Mr- SINCLAIR:	Will the minister say
why he resorted to the terms of section 21 in order to appoint men whose salaries were $1,000, $1,200 and $1,300 without competitive examination and why they were not appointed in the regular way under the Civil Service Act?

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: Some were above the age. As the hon. gentleman knows, section 14 of the Civil Service Act provides that a person to be appointed under the Act must be less than thirty-five years of age. If he is over thirty-five he cannot be appointed, but if he is a technical man the Civil Service Commission will issue a certificate in the case of a man who is over thirty-five. There is another provision of the Civil Service Act that a man should be in the country three years before appointment. Some of these men can\e from the old country. They were Edinburgh and Glasgow University men and they had not been in the country three years at the time of their appointment. That is the only way they could be appointed under section 21. All these are technical men although their salaries are not very large. They satisfied the Civil Service Commission that they were perfectly qualified and that was the only way in which they could be appointed to their respective positions.

I should like to know from the minister the policy of the department. I am quite well aware that wThere an official joins the army he draws his civil salary and also his military salary in full if he enlisted prior to the 1st of November, 1915. I have no objection to make in the ease of a man who goes to the front and fights for his country, but I would like to know if it is the policy of the department to continue paying these civil servants who joined the army prior to the 1st of November, 1915, where they are simply appointed to clerkships in Ottawa or in England and do not go near the front, who take no more risk than they, did up in the civil service -offices on the hill?

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext:
It is not the policy of this department to have men . who joined prior to the 1st of November, 1915, but had not crossed the ocean, continue to receive their full salary. I do not think we have a single instance of that nature. We had one case of a man whose services were especially asked for by the Department of Militia. He was doing some particular work at Halifax, and we were asked to allow the Militia Department to retain him on their pay list.
We have since ascertained that his services were not as essential as they had been, so, at our request, he has returned to his civil duties.

That answer is quite satisfactory. Is the same rule followed by all the departments of Government? Perhaps the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Sir George Foster), who is leading the House, may be able to>
answer that question,

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: I am sorry to say I was talking with my friend when the subject matter was brought up. I think my hon. friend knows pretty well what is done.

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: I have heard that this was the policy generally. Whether there are any exceptions to it or not, I do not know, but I think the policy I have adopted in my department is the policy that is universal throughout the service. There may be some individual cases that I am not aware of.

The minister told the committee just a few minutes ago the superintendent of Jasper park was drawing his salary from the department, although his military duties were entirely confined to this side of the water; and the minister gave us to understand that he would have continued to draw his salary as superintendent of Jasper park, and would, in fact, be drawing it to-day, although his military services are entirely on this side of the water, if he had not himself requested to be taken off the pay list. Therefore in that instance the minister's policy was to pay the full salary when the duties were on this side of the water and did not involve service at the front.

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext:
The difference is that
Colonel Maynard Rogers did go across the ocean; he did not remain in Canada. It was only after he returned to Canada that he was struck off the pay roll. He enlisted prior to November 1, 1915, and was in the enjoyment of his full salary. He went across the ocean and was paid full salary until after he came back, and he was still retained in the Militia Department; but he voluntarily came and asked to be stricken off the pay roll and we did not want to keep him on when he did not desire to be retained. We would not have kept him on the roll if we had not been especially informed by the Militia Department that his services were required.

That puts the thing differently. The minister gave us to understand

a few minutes ago that Colonel Rogers was removed from the pay roll at his own request, and not as a matter of policy of the Interior Department.

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: I did not say the latter, I said at his own request.

The minister gave the committee to understand that had he not requested to be taken off the pay Toll he would still have, been on the pay roll. That was the impression conveyed to my mind, and I think to the House. As to his having crossed the ocean, while he did cross the ocean, I am not aware that he ever rendered any active military service; but, in any case, the point is that he is not rendering any active military service now, and that is the condition mentioned by my hon. friend from Assiniboia (Mr. Turriff).

I think the minister put too limited an interpretation on my question. My question was with respect to civil servants who were working either on this side of the water or as clerks in the paymaster's and similar offices in England, the men who never went to the firing line, who took no more risk whether in England or in Canada than if they had remained in their offices on the hill. I shall not press for an answer to-night, but I should like to know if those men who enlisted prior to November 1, 1915, and have been employed in clerical positions in England or in Canada, are receiving two salaries. I think it is absurd that a man drawing a big, fat salary should serve in the Department of Militia or in England as a clerk and draw two large salaries at the expense of the people. I would like a clear, definite answer as to the policy of the Government in that matter.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: Before November 1, 1915, the man who enlisted did so on the understanding that he should enjoy both salaries. Would my hon. friend say that 'because when he went overseas he was found to be more useful or necessary in the clerical part of the militia work, we should violate the condition upon which he enlisted? To the man who enlisted after the date mentioned, that condition not being part of the contract, so to speak, the double pay would not be given. The question rests a good deal upon whether or not the man enlisted upon the condition that he should get both salaries.

When the man enlisted he was supposed to go to the front and fight

for his country, hut in hundreds of casds, through influence and political pull, men have secured appointments to clerical positions, say, in England, and have been there ever since the war started. Those who do that are not carrying out' the agreement that was made, because they enlisted to go to the front and they have not done so. They are drawing two fat salaries, without taking any risk whatever, whereas the man who enlisted later, goes to the front and risks his life, gets only $1.10 a day.

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: In many cases we do not know what work these men are doing after they cross the ocean. We are not in a position to know who is and who is not doing clerical work in England. Besides, I believe that the policy over there is to appoint to such positions men who have been at the front and who have returned wounded or invalided, thus allowing men physically fit for military duty to go to the front. I agree with my hon. friend who is leading the House that we made an agreement with these men who enlisted prior to the date mentioned, and it would be rather a breach of contract were we now, simply because they were detained in London to perform certain work, to strike them off the list and not pay them according to the arrangement made.

A man drawing $2,000
a. year in Canada gets a commission, goes to the old country and through influence secures a position there, where he is absolutely safe from any danger except mere chance of a bomb falling from a Zeppelin. He draws $3,000 or $4,000 for work that can be done just as well by the man getting $1.10 a day. I ask the minister if he thinks that is fair.

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: I do not think that there are such cases; I have not heard of any.
I have heard of a great many.

The question is, is he on active service? If I understand the militia rule, he enlisted for active service, and if he is employed as a clerk in an office in London, I do not think it can be said that he is on active service.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: He enlisted for overseas service.

The evidence that there are a great many men in that position is found in the statement of the ex-Minister of Militia, who tells us that he was able

to ran the London office with 30 employees, bnt that since the matter was taken out of hi3 hands over 600 employees have been required, costing the country an enormous sum of money each year. I assume that most of those employees are soldiers of the kind mentioned-Canadian adventurers, who, professing to go to the front, found their way into the London office. If we can believe the statement made by the exMinister of Militia, this is a matter of great importance. The principle cannot be laid down that these men are employed on active service, when they are simply doing clerical work in a London office, .and a man doing that kind of work is not, under the contract that was made with him, entitled to two salaries.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext:
I had the idea, before I went to London, that our Records Office was costing us a very large amount of money, and I think I expressed that sentiment. When I w>as there I made it my business to go through those offices, and I do not care who states that the clerical work there can be done !by 30, 40 or 50 men, I say that it is absolutely impossible. A complete record has to be kept of the men that we have at the front and in different parts of England, of their pay and of all other details; their transfer from one regiment or from one division to another- everything has to be taken cognizance of and becomes a matter of record. I went through room after room; I examined their books and saw their methods of doing things, and I came away with the impression that these men were busily engaged at a necessary woTk. The army must be looked upon as a whole. You must have good subsidiary officers and workers as well as good fighters. The man Who enlists for overseas service enlists for whatever service the army officers and authorities consider that he is best fitted for. Men are brought back from the front 'because of their special ability to perform what we call clerical work, but what is so important and affects so vitally the well-being of the army that the very best men are required. I should be very sorry to have the impression going out that we are employing thousands of men over there where 30, 40 or 50 could do the work. I do not think that would be a right impression to go to the country. This much I do know: that of late the offices have been combed out over and over again in order that every man who can be spared from that absolutely necessary work may go to the front and take his part of the burden of active warfare,
in his place those that have had their turn at the front and have had the casualties, are brought in to do the work. The impression that exists now that there are so many able bodied men who have never gone to ,the front, who do not want to go to the front and yet who are able enough to go to the front, but that are kept in London through favour or anything else-that impression is a wrong one.

The impression did not originate on this side; it originated with my right hon. friend's colleague who made the positive statement. Perhaps if my right hon. friend knows that that statement is not true he will tell us just how many men be has employed in the London office and how many of those men are soldiers who have volunteered for active service at the front. We do not know; we are going only on the statement made by the ex-minister, a gentleman who had the information and who ought to know. If there is any man in Canada who ought to know these facts, it is the exJMinister of Militia.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: I have not seen that statement.
If the minister will look at the exjminister's statement, be will find that the ex-minister had made that statement.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: I would not be inclined to think that he had made that statement.

I have no doubt he made the statement that, in an office where there were formerly thirty men-and he gave the name of the man in charge of the office- now, under the influence of the Minister of Finance and the management of the Minister of Militia Overseas, the number had grown to over 600, costing the country $6,000,000 a year. That is nut my statement, it is the statement of the ex-minister. I do not know whether it is true or not.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: I have not seen that statement.

It has also been,stated publicly that no less than 45,000 or 50,000 men who have gone overseas, were not able to go to the front because they were medically unfit. If any of those men who were medically unfit have found their way into the offices in London, I think their doing so would disqualify them from getting the double pay. It is for the Government to clear up the statements of the ex-Minister

of Militia and not we on this side of the House.

The question is not how much work is required in the offices in London; it is whether the men whom we are paying here in this Dominion of Canada for the services they are rendering us, are drawing pay for other services that they are rendering and that are not the services we understood or expected they would render when we made the bargain with them. There is no question at all that this Government did not make a bargain with its officials that it would give them double pay for the purpose of enabling them to do clerical work in London. There is no doubt but what my -hon. friend from Assini-boia (Mr. Turriff) has said is the absolute root and basis of the understanding that these men were going forward to risk their lives for the welfare of their country, and that it was because of that consideration alone that they were given this extra remuneration. If for any reason, whether on account of their own fault or that of anyone else, they have not fulfilled that condition, this country has no right- to give them double pay, and when we are giving them double pay, we are doing an injustice to ourselves and to those who are honestly trying to -serve their country. It may be true that these men are good men in the clerical .offices in London, but there are others just -as good men who are -able to do clerical work; and if they are able to do clerical work and not able to go to the front, then their place is here -and not in London, that is, if we have need of their services in our departments. They should be either here or at the front if they are drawing double pay. If they are not able to go to the front, then -they -should be drawing only single pay and they should be here if they are going to draw pay from us for the services they are rendering us. We cannot undertake to provide for the exigencies of our Civil Service here and also for the exigencies of a Civil Service over in England. The latter is a matter that can be attended to by itself. Our business here is -to see that the work of the Civil Service is attended to and to pay for that civil service, and if we have made extra bargains with some of our civil servants in regard to military services, when they fulfill the necessary conditions, they are entitled to the extra consideration we promise them, hut if they do not fulfill those conditions, they are not entitled to that extra consideration. I 
for one call upon this Government to take measures to see that only those men who fulfill the condition upon which they w'ere promised that extra pay, receive that extra pay, and to see that those who do not fulfill that condition do not get that extra pay. I have already mentioned here to-day the case of a gentleman drawing $2,400 a year as superintendent of Jasper Park, who takes a position as colonel in the overseas forces, goes to England and draws pay as an overseas colonel, but who never does a day's duty at the front, never renders any valuable service to the military authorities, and who comes back to Canada and still draws that double pay.
Mr. ROCHE-: Is the hon. gentleman quite right in stating that he did not render valuable military services?
I am quite right.

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext:
What work was he doing?
Mr. OLI^ ER: I do not care to bring it up here in the House, but he was like a great many more so-called military men, who went over to England, who had neither right nor reason to be called military men and who did not render good service. This man comes back to Canada and still draws double pay although on the evidence he was not considered fit for military service at the front., If such a prominent case can occur, we can easily believe that hundreds of such cases have occurred, and we call upon the Government not to defend that condition, but to take measures to see that that condition does not exist because it is absolutely a breach of faith with the people of this country.

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext:
It is only right that I
should make this statement in regard to the gentleman whom the -hon. member is criticising. I remember, after 'the hon. gentleman 'discussed this question last session, having taken, the matter up with the military authorities, and the information received was that Colonel Maynard Rogers had rendered very valuable -military service in England in that, as I understand, he was engaged in training troops in some of the large camps. The report from the Militia Department was that he had rendered splendid service. It is only right that I should make that statement in justice to the gentleman.
The minister would not expect any other kind of report from the Militia Department.

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext:
In regard to other men
going overseas and. doing clerical -work, I understand that the paymaster of a battalion does not go to the firing line, yet we .pay him double pay if he goes over with his battalion- Does the hon. gentleman think that because a paymaster is doing some clerical work or looking after the financing of bis battalion and not engaged in the firing line, he should not be paid his full civil pay if he enlisted prior to the first of November, 1915?
Is the paymaster of a battalion in France resident in England?

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext:
Why does the
hon. member differentiate between England and France if soldiers are not engaged in the firing line?

A paymaster is with his
battalion; it does not matter whether he is at the firing line or not; he is on active service. I am very sorry to find that the leader of the House and the Minister of the Interior take the attitude to-day of defending a condition that is absolutely indefensible, defending an absolute breach of faith with the people of this country.
I am very much surprised that they should take that attitude.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: My hon. friend need not expend any of his sorrow on me with reference to that. The position I take is simply this: In respect to those men who under certain conditions enlisted to go overseas for such service as was required and who have fulfilled these conditions, there is an obligation upon us to fill our part of the bargain. The difference between my hon. friend and myself is, I suppose, this: he says that the condition of their enlistment before that date was that they should go to the firing line.
No, pardon me.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: That they should go into active service, then.
Our undertaking to continue their pay was on the understanding they were risking their lives in our behalf.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext:
I do not know that they entered into a contract to risk their lives. They entered into a contract in this way: they enlisted for active service overseas, whatever that service might be. I do not think there was anything in the contract that they were to risk their lives in going over. Whatever was the duty which was assigned to the man who enlisted for
overseas, that was the duty he was to perform, and if he performed that duty under the conditions laid down before November 15, he was to receive his full pay. If we *were to set out anew and the question was brought up as to whether men should receive double pay who were simply doing clerical work in London, I would not hesitate for a single moment to say that it was the man who went right into the trenches that should get the double pay.
To pay expenses connected with Water Power investigation and reports in Manitoba, Saskatchewan, Alberta and the Railway Belt in B.C., $159,000.

This is a time when there is certainly very little likelihood of important investments in the development of water power. It seems to me this is another item in the Estimates of the Interior Department that might very well be eliminated or very greatly reduced under present conditions. If we are pursuing a policy of saving with a view to meeting our enormous war obligations, I think it is only right that I should take the responsibility of pointing out all those instances where it seems to me the Government have fallen very far short of their full duty.
For surveys and works under the Irrigation Act, etc., including $400 for P. Marchand as auditor of disbursements made by companies acquiring lands under the Irrigation System, $174,000.
What is the nature of this expenditure?

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext:
The following are the particulars :	

For the fiscal year 1916-1917, the estimate was reduced by $68,350, or 25 per cent, while the estimate now submitted shows a further reduction of $26,000 or 13 per cent; the present estimate is thus 35 per cent less than the appropriation for the year 1915-16. The sum asked for will provide for carrying on only that work that is considered absolutely essential, including:
1.	The maintenance of the permanent office and field staff at Ottawa and Calgary. The reduction in appropriation will necessitate the discharge of several present members of the staff and the rearrangement of the work so as to provide for its efficient conduct with fewer men.
2.	The inspection of existing and proposed irrigation and water supply projects. Such inspections are required by law to determine the feasibility of proposed projects and to ascertain whether or not those who have been authorized to construct works are proceeding with due diligence and whether licenses are utilizing, or are in a position to utilize, the water to which they are entitled by license. A considerable saving will be effected by combining in certain districts the duties of

stream measurements and irrigation inspections. This is an innovation, but it is believed that these duties can be combined without loss of efficiency.
3.	The continuation of hydrometric or stream measurement work. The determination of the quantity of water available in the streams of the prairie provinces is the basis of all irrigation and water supply development and is absolutely essential to the proper administration of the Irrigation Act. Stream measurements must be carried on continuously for a long period of years in order to be of real value, and any interruption seriously affects the value of the records. This work has been carried on systematically since 190S and has been gradually extended so as to cover practically all streams in the southern part of the Provinces of Alberta and Saskatchewan and the principal streams in the north. Regular measurements are made otf the flow of all streams during the summer, or open water period, and after the winter freeze-up the districts are re-arranged and the flow of the principal streams is measured under ice conditions throughout the winter months. The department has frequently been urged to extend the scope of this work and it is believed that the public interest warrants its continuation and expense in spite of the necessity for the strictest economy. The plans for the (coming year do not provide for any expansion of the work, but on the contrary some stations are to be temporarily abandoned and the work will be so arranged as to effect a considerable saving without materially affecting the efficiency of the service.
4.	The continuation of experimental work to' determine the proper "duty of water," and to demonstrate the benefits of irrigated farming. This experimental work has not yet been carried on for a long enough period to yield definite or reliable data upon which to base any revision of the "duty of water." The existing duty' is acknowledged to be too low and should be raised, but it is believed to be unwise to attempt revision without reliable data obtained under Canadian conditions of soil and climate. For this reason our experimental work should be continued.
5.	The continuation of the work of soil analysis in order to determine the suitability of certain soils for irrigated agriculture. This work has now been carried on for several years in collaboration with the Dominion chemist of the Department of Agriculture. It was begun, primarily for the purpose of excluding from irrigation projects areas so strongly impregnated with alkali as to render them unfit for cultivation, but it has been found necessary to extend the scope of the work to include a systematic study of the changes in soils due to the continued practice of irrigation, so as to determine what crops may be most profitably grown and how certain soils may be treated so as to preserve their fertility and prevent their becoming waterlogged and sour. In general, it may be said that no new work is being undertaken. The scope of permanent work is being somewhat restricted and so arranged as to effect a considerable saving. Very few salary increases have been provided for, and these only in exceptionally deserving cases (six in all). No general salary increases have been granted since the outbreak of the war.
fMr. Roche. ]
Are any of the private schemes mentioned in the memorandum under construction at the present time?

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: I have not that information, but I could get it for the next sitting.

As regards private applications for the use of water and the establishment of irrigation systems, I quite agree that the expenditure is necessary, whatever it may foe, but a great deal of the work mentioned in the memorandum is something that I think could be postponed for a time at any rate. That is something that can be postponed for a time at any rate. I wish to know what is the really necessary work of development in that country. I fancy it could be paid for with a small proportion of the vote.

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext:
We have a trained staff,
and it would not do to disband that staff. We must keep them at work. Last year the hon. member for Medicine Hat (Mr. Buchanan) strongly urged us, notwithstanding our declaration for economy, to extend this work considerably in .connection with some projects for irrigation in his district.

I have nothing to say
against expenditure for actual irrigation work, but I wanted to know what amount was required for that.

How much land was
granted last year under the Irrigation Act?

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: I think a return was asked ' for on that subject-, and that it was brought down. But I do not recollect the figures. Canadian National Parks. $300,000.

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext:
This is a reduction of
549,670 from last year.

About what amount is
appropriated for Jasper Park?

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: Fifty-four thousand dollars.

What are the items of
expenditure*?

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: Fire and game protection, fire-fighting, maintenance of roads and trails, new buildings-
What new buildings?

This is not a large item,
it is for stables.
Are there any revenues from the park?

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext:
Of course the principal return from our national parks is the tourist

trade. I quoted figures last year showing, as I recollect them, that about 100,000 tourists had visited the national parks last year. This traffic, of course, brings in a great deal of money. Our parks are very attractive and advertise Canada everywhere. They are becoming very well known in the United States. Since the outbreak of the war in Europe many American tourists are coming to Canada.
Has the department considered what effect it will have on the tourist traffic to have the rails of the Grand Trunk Pacific to Jasper Park takeu up and shipped away?

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: I do not know from what portion of the road the rails have been taken. I understand that the Canadian Northern and the Grand Trunlc Pacific run side by side for miles, two lines where one would serve all purposes.

The beautiful scenery of Jasper Park, of course, is a great attraction. But tourists do not live on scenery; they have to eat and they have to sleep. 'In order to have a successful tourist traffic there must be accommodation for the tourists, and up to the present time the hotel accommodation for tourists in Jasper Park has been very limited and inadequate. I am given to understand that one reason has been that the departmental
10 p.m. authorities set a standard of hotel buildings that the business does not warrant. I quite .agree that proper buildings should be erected in the park, but until business is established judgment must be exercised in imposing restrictions. You can only get such investment of money in buildings as the business is likely to give a return upon, and to impose too onerous restrictions is simply to prevent any accommodation being provided, and so to prevent the park from being used for the purpose for which it was intended.

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: The hon. gentleman, I suppose, Tefers to a minimum value for the hotel buildings. I may say that no minimum value is fixed for hotel buildings in Jasper Park, but there is a minimum for private residences.

I am afraid the hon. minister is under the wrong impression. In any case, there is urgent need for tourist accommodation in Jasper Park. A moderate measure of accommodation would be a great advantage, but that moderate measure of accommodation cannot be secured if undue requirement is made in the matter of expenditure, and so the usefulness of the park is to a great extent lost.
What is being done with the surplus of buffalo being raised in Buffalo Park?

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: There has been no disposition of the surplus as yet.

Last year I asked the minister if he was going to fulfill the undertaking that was given some years ago about sending some buffalo down to the Moose Mountain reserve. The Government bought the land and paid for it and the reason given last year why the buffalo had not been removed to it was that some one had reported that the land was not suitable. There is no use of any person reporting that to me because I know all about the land; it is perfectly suitable. The Government bought and paid for the land some years ago, they advertised for tenders for putting up the fence, but it was never gone on with and the land is lying there idle. The department have more buffalo in Northern Alberta than they need and it would be a good work to send 20 or 30 of them down to the park. There are no buffalo in southern Saskatchewan at all. Formerly that was the home of the buffalo. When, on occasion, the minister is asked to do anything of this kind he pleads economy. I notice that he has reduced his estimates by quite a sum this year and I give him a considerable amount of credit for it although I think the reduction could have been carried very much further on several items. It seems to me that to ask for a vote of $2,879,000 under this head is not showing a great deal of economy. The putting of some buffalo in the park is a matter of a very few miles of fence, and it would not cost much money. The minister has three men now working on the reserve as forest inspectors and fire rangers where formerly one was considered sufficient when there was a great deal more timber than there is at the present time. It would not entail any additional cost to the Government to keep some buffalo there. I would like to ask the minister if he has forgotten his promise that he would take this into his very favourable consideration.

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext:
The reason I have not actively taken it into my consideration, that is acted upon it practically, is simply fire desire to economize. The hon. gentleman has given me credit for having reduced my estimates. So I have. I have reduced

them very materially on nearly every item. I have reduced my estimates for this coming year by not far from $1,000,000, or over $900,000. It would cost considerable money to move a portion of the herd of buffalo down to where the hon. gentleman wants them. It would involve the building of a fence, the employment of the necessary men and a superintendent and the providing of winter food, etc.
My hon. friend has men there now with practically nothing to do.

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: There is nobody on salary.

The minister told us half an hour ago when we were talking about timber reserves that he had three men there. They could look after the buffalo. Their principal job in connection with the timber is to draw their pay. While my hon. friend has done fairly well in cutting down his estimates by $400,000, he could very well have cut off an extra $800,000 and left his expenditure at $2,000,000 which would be ample in these times when we are supposed to have economy in every place but the Government departments.

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: But you are asking me to increase the expenditure.

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: Nearly 2,400 in Buffalo park.

How many in the other
one?

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: In Moose park 17. These are the figures: Rocky Mountain park, 13; Buffalo park 2,399; Elk Island park, 134, making a total of 2,546.
How many other animals are there?

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: Moose, 73; elk, 153, and mule deer, 180.

The Moose Mountain reserve, which is in southern Saskatchewan, is the only place for some hundreds of miles in two or three directions where there is any considerable body of timber or water. It is a great resort for people in the southern portion of Saskatchewan. I have been at the reserve on a Sunday and I have seen 200 automobiles there in which people have come for a distance of 50, 75 and 100 miles to spend the day. I would be satisfied if my hon. friend would fence what was

necessary to take care of ten or fifteen buffalo. I dp not want my hon. friend to do much but surely he could spare ten head of buffalo out of the 2,000 he has. It would not cost very much.
Engraving, lithographing, printing and preparation of maps, plans and kindred publications of the Dominion, including necessary materials for same, $66,100.

There is a reduction of
$10,050.	'
Mr. OLIVER; Does this lithographing include the cost of making homestead maps?

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: Yes.
How soon may the edition of the homestead maps for this year be expected to be available and which .section is likely to be out first?

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: The edition is in course of preparation but I cannot exactly tell the date at which it will be available for distribution. It will be expedited as much as possible.

I have an inquiry from
the Alberta Association of Municipalities in regard to taxation on lands held in reservation for the Hudson Bay Company. The association protests against this reservation of lands to belong to the Hudson Bay Company inasmuch as that reservation prevents them levying taxation on those lands. I have addressed the resolution of the association to the minister, hut possibly he will be able - to make a statement to the House in regard to the situation as to this reservation otf the Hudson Bay lands ' and their freedom from taxation at the present time.

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext:
The hon. gentleman wrote me and I am having the information prepared in the department -and will send it to the hon. member in a day or two. I understand that there is a considerable reservation from which the Hudson Bay Company is to select land. There have been a number of their lands in some of our forest reserves and we have been getting them to exchange those lands for other lands, and have placed a certain reservation on the lands from which they are to make selection. There has been a little hitch in this respect:	In the past it has
been their privilege to go and make their selection o<f other Dominion lands from reservations irrespective otf what their value might be. The members of the Council were of the opinion that there ought to he a little better investigation into She nature

of those lands and their value before having any exchange made and they ''suggested that we should take it up with the Hudson Bay Company to see if we could not get them to accept lands [DOT] of a similar v-alue. In the past it has been lands of similar area, but we might be receiving in exchange lands much inferior to those that they would select. For that reason we have taken the matter up recently with the Hudson Bay Company to see if they would not accept lands of similar value. The Hudson Bay Company are not anxious to do that. In the first place, they say it would be more expensive, having to value the lands; they would have to put on a valuator and so would we. They think that, inasmuch as the exchange is being made at our solici-ation, they ought to be free to select any available Dominion lands irrespective of value. The matter is being taken up now and will be dealt with as expeditiously as possible.

From the same source
there is a resolution in reference to the accumulation of taxes against pre-emptions . or homesteads which have reverted to the Crown. As I remember the purport of the resolution, it asks that where local taxes have accrued against a pre-emption or homestead that has finally reverted to the Crown, those taxes be held as a lien against that land, to be met by the subsequent entrant. That is, in effect they ask that the local taxes be put in the same position as improvements made by the original entrant who forfeits his homestead.

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: That might result in leaving a Iqt of land on our hands.
The suggestion has been passed on by me to the minister, and I have asked him if he could make a statement upon it.

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext:
I have not given that point much consideration. I can see certain difficulties in connection with it, but I will give it consideration.
