speakeroldname: The DEPUTY SPEAKER (Mr. J. H. Rainville) (Speaking in English):
speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
subtopic: THE FRENCH WAR MISSION TO THE UNITED STATES.
subsubtopic: SPECIAL, SITTING OF THE HOUSE ADDRESSED BY M. VIVIANI.
speechtext:
Monsieur Viviani:	1 am proud to be in
the position as Deputy Speaker of this House to express the welcome of the people of Canada to you on this happy occasion. We all appreciate the fact that you have not missed the opportunity afforded by your important mission in America of visiting Canada, now a great' democracy, thanks to the genius of Great Britain, and upon which a deep imprint has been left by the France of old days.
Allow me, in the absence of His Honour the Speaker of the House of Commons, who deeply regrets his inability to be present, to thank you and to say that your presence in our midst stimulates our desire to help in the war, whilst it also carries with it a' lesson of the highest significance. We cannot forget that love of freedom and the desire to promote all generous causes have ever been among the basic principles upon which your country has built its civilization. There are no people in the world who more than those of France love truth,

justice, equality, and have more strenuously fought for their triumph.
Your arrival in Ottawa has assumed the importance of a public festival. You will find here nine provinces federally united under the same flag, having three oceans for their boundaries and enjoying complete liberty under the segis of the British Crown and under the political institutions which have been established by the British constitution.
The admirable verse of your poet Henri de Bornier. "Every man has two countries his own and France," seems peculiarly to apply to us now that our sons have blended their blood in the struggles and successes of bitter warfare. Our eyes are turning more and more towards your country, where thousands of Canadian volunteers have made the supreme sacrifice on the altar of liberty and fraternity. One of our youngest colleagues, Colonel BakeT, member for Brome, has fallen on the field of honour. Another, Dr. Beland, who was'formerly a minister of the Crown, is now lingering in a German prison; twelve others are now at the front; the sons of about fifty senators and members have enlisted, and some of them will never return.
It is a long martyrdom that France 16 now suffering, but her energy, pertinacity and heroism will bring victory to her flag in this brutal war which has been cruelly thrust upon her. In the darkest days, your glorious nation has ever held the proud position which the genius and intellect of her sons have secured for her in the world's civilization. Their portion of the common sacrifice is indeed very large, hut we hope and know that it will result in a victory which shall not only be glorious but permanent.
You will in a few days leave the American continent and return to your partly devastated France, where Canadians of different origins aTe now fighting shoulder to shoulder with your fellow citizens. Kindly convey to France the testimony of the admiration and sympathy which this war has inspired in our hearts for her noble ideals; tell her that you have seen on this Canadian soil a young nation which has stayed its material development for the purpose of assisting the world to vanquish that militarism which has already produced terrible results in Europe and has so seriously threatened the freedom of mankind.
We welcome you most cordially among us and wish you personally happiness and prosperity, trusting that your visit to
[The Deputy Speaker.]
Canada may be one of the pleasant memories of your mission.
In this welcome I feel confident that I express the united sentiment of all the people of Canada.	.
(Translation into English.)

subtopic: THE FRENCH WAR MISSION TO THE UNITED STATES.
subsubtopic: SPECIAL, SITTING OF THE HOUSE ADDRESSED BY M. VIVIANI.
speechtext:
As has been said by your Speaker, Mr. Eainville, in his eloquent address, we could not possibly have passed so close to your country without having an ardent wish to visit it and to pay our respects to its citizens, with whose history our own is so intimately connected.
Hardly had we reached Canada than we, the members of the French delegation, were the object of the most enthusiastic welcome. And as a crowning success, gentlemen. you were so kind as to confer on my fellow-citizens and myself the supreme honour of a reception within the precincts of this House, and there could be no greater boon, no higher honour, no greater joj, than this provisional adoption into your community.
You may rest assured that our fellow-citizens in far away France, when they are apprised to-morrow or the day after, of the honour which has been conferred upon us, will- have towards you a high feeling of gratitude.
You have just requested us, Mr. Speaker, ;iot to forget the reception now tendered to us, and through us, to France; allow me, Sir, to thank you. That debt of gratitude which we owe to your great country, and which the great historical events in which we have participated in common, can only have the effect of increasing-that debt impressed us particularly on that day when we saw passing through the streets of Paris your admirable Canadian soldiers proudly bearing on itiheir helmets the Maiple Leaf. (Cheering). At thait tragic hour we realized that your motto of former days-" I remember "-was no vain formula, no mere catchword.
Yes, you have remembered, and indeed it is something that strikes one with admiration to witness how this feeling of gratitude, as a rule a personal feeling lying in the depths of the human heart and conscience, diffuses itself throughout democracies and becomes a collective feeling which makes for the greatness of the nation as a whole. I remember, and we have proof that you have also remembered. First of all, your generosity towards France is unfathomable. Of course, I could not hut omit important facts and be perhaps unfair were I to attempt an enumeration of your generous

deeds, and of all that you have done for France: field hospitals without number; the hospital at St. Cloud, in which you have reserved 1,300 beds for French patients, and other hospitals everywhere established, with a staff of Canadian nurses and medical superintendents.
I need not point especially to the supreme sacrifice, to which you have just given a pious thought in recalling that some members of this House have fallen at the front in'this holy cause; that some are held prisoners in Germany, that you gentlemen of the Parliament of Canada have given fifty of your sons who, without hesitation have gone over to resist in the name of truth and -justice the most formidable avalanche which barbarity has ever let loose on the civilized world. (Applause.)
Yes, Sir, your Canadians have fought along with English and French troops, without paying any heed to racial differences. Under the flags of all the Allies they have all shown a similar courage. It must not be forgotten that in the month .of February of 1915, at Ypres, in the north of France) near the Belgian frontier, in a country devastated by floods, after the terrific assault of the German soldiers by means of asphyxiating gases-Germany, the country that has caused science to swerve from its true ends, and, instead of pouring its benefits upon mankind, has visited humanity with manifold evils and crimes-that same Germany has had to meet your Canadian soldiers. On that terrific day, your sons, rising in their might, saved the situation. (Cheering.)
And throughout many battles, throughout numerous and recent victories, the soldiers of Canada stood up heroically against the foe. Even at this moment, we have before our eyes your boys, so alert, so athletic, so brave, the first to storm, victoriously carrying their flag to that ridge of Vimy which was reputed to be dimpregnialble. (Cheering.)
Hail, to all these soldiers; let us bow our heads reverently before those who fight, those who suffer and those who have laid down their lives for their country. They had a clear perception of what their action meant; when they left this country they were well aware that it was not only Great Britain that they were called upon to defend, that it was not only France that they were going to protect against the attacks of invaders;-their clear vision upturned towards Heaven, detected the higher object; they were well aware that it was the sacred cause of humanity,
of democracy, and of justice that they were defending. (Cheering.)
Still labouring under the impression left by such glorious and recent events, we have come here to pay you a visit. Your enthusiastic welcome only serves to increase the bitterness of my regrets, as I reflect on its inevitable brevity; but I am confident that you will be at one with me when I state that depth of feeling should not be measured by the length of a visit, but rather by the persistence of the feelings which are thereby instilled in the heart and in the mind. Such assurances of our feelings which I bring to you, I would much have liked, after visiting your beautiful Capital, to carry to other cities; it 'would have afforded me great pleasure to have visited Toronto, Quebec, Montreal, but our time is limited, and I beg that you may excuse the shortness of our stay, thinking only of the sincerity of the feelings expressed in our message to you.
It would have been a great satisfaction to me to travel at leisure over this admirable country, thinking and dreaming over past events in your history which, at many points, is interlocked with our own national history.
In coming to this country I desire to pay a tribute to Great Britain, that land of freedom, whose sons, wherever they go, bring with them emancipation and liberty; under every sky her mission is not to reduce men to slavery, but to awaken consciences and arouse determinations. I should have assured Great Britain, our noble ally, of our gratitude for having rallied to a man to the rescue of France in this, her supreme hour, because forsooth British statesmen had been parties to a treaty guaranteeing Belgian neutrality; because England's pledge was not to be denied; because a nation's honour has not two codes, nor a double morality, and because every country should take up arms and fight with all its might to redeem her promise.
I desire also, to recall the memory of our ancestors, those Frenchmen who came to this country in olden times and who seem to have brought to this soil all the eleganee of manners and the beauty of France and Normandie. I am happy to note in their scions the ancient and strong qualities which are the reputed and proud characteristics of our race. To them I owe my thanks for having maintained in all its purity and perfection that noble French, which language to-day resounds throughout

the universe, which you, Mr. Speaker, speak so admirably, and which you know in its absolute purity, partaking as it does of the limpidity of a stream and the resistance of a metal. (Applause).
It would have been a pleasure to me had I time to note on the bronzed faces of your country people the familiar traits of their brothers, our French peasants; and bow acknowledgment to the virtues which they share in common; thrift, assiduity to the daily task, steadfastness, and everything \yhieh contributes to the strength, the valour, and the fame of a nation.
My time is limited, and I must beg your p.ardon for abbreviating my remarks. However, 1 would not be doing justice to the utterances which fell a moment ago from the lips of your Speaker if, at this very moment, and from this time, from this high situation you have assigned to me, though a stranger among you, I did not, following in the footsteps of the speaker who preceded me, attempt through time and space to solve the serious problems brought on us by the war, including the very carrying out of that war.
In the first place, what was the origin of that war? Who is responsible for having started it? You mentioned it in your speech, Mr. Speaker, that bloody war was let loose on us by the whim of an absolute ruler, a ruler whose will is the only law, who governs heedless of parliament or ministerial responsibilities. It was let loose by the pride and madness of a whole people. It was let loose to destroy the free democracies and peace-loving peoples of the world.
Who among the peoples of the earth were more attached to universal peace than Great Britain and France? France had been vanquished in 1871-and it is no longer an humiliation to us to recall that defeat, since in the meantime we have retrieved ourselves and find ourselves once more in a position to face our enemies. (Prolonged applause). Such was our liking for peace that while with tearful eyes we looked over the war-ridden boundary, while -we peered over the border at our provinces of Alsace and Lorraine, and while we carried in our breast a bleeding wound which could not be healed, yet so as not to trouble the world's peace, though not forgetful of the past, we kept still. Such was our attitude.
Then, as regards Great Britain, which German slanders charged with having brought on the war, she had not even thought of establishing military conscription; she had not provided a fighting

machine, lacking which war becomes impossible; she was thinking of universal peace only, and of providing work for and insuring the freedom of nations.
Both these nations were attacked, France, Great Britain, and also Russia. It was a challenge sent out to the whole civilized world, and then it was a question, not as to whether we were going to fight for the acquisition of territory, not as to whether we should recover sections of provinces, but as to whether free men would be allowed to enjoy the warmth and light of liberty. (Applause).
Such is the great struggle that is going on between an arrogant autocracy, which already we have struck down on the battlefield; an autocracy, bent on ruling over the world, and democracy, whose sole aim is to regenerate it. Such is' the great struggle between absolute rulers, who consider as mere possessions the peoples over whom they hold sway, who aim at enslaving men's bodies, and democracy, whose object, is to uplift the mind, the conscience and the soul.
And notice what wonderful changes have taken place in Great Britain and France. Some time previous to the war those two nations had come closer to one another and had concluded, many years ago, the emitanite cor diale. This reference to the entente cordiale concluded between Frame and Great Britain reminds me necessarily of your former governor, Lord Lansdowne, whom I had the honour to meet in London some years ago, one of the keenest and most refined minds in Great Britain, and who, no doubt, because he had long lived an-jong you and because he had come to know France through knowing Canada, came back to Great Britain with a desire to establish l'entente cordiale and bring the two countries closer together.
Here I am bound to pay my respects to the memory of Edward VII who was the enthusiastic medium of bringing together those two great democratic and free nations, because his clear insight into conditions generally had satisfied him that such a result was possible and in order. Neither can I. proceed any further without paying homage to his successor on the throne who with a strong hand in that tragic moment of history brought about the practical results implied in the entente cordiale as formerly concluded.
What an admirable example was set to us by those two countries. Great Britain had remained aloof from conscription; she had applied her whole activity to forwarding in-

dustry, trade, and building up her navy. And when the hour of danger came, when she felt that a few thousand men would not be sufficient to resist the onslaught; when she realized that the war would be won not solely through the bravery of her children, through the courage of her soldiers, but that munitions, guns, and munition factories would be indispensable; then as by a miracle at the call of the Government, not only in Great Britain but in Ireland and throughout its possessions and colonies- for the British colonies to Germany's great -surprise rallied to their mother country in the hour of danger-not only munition factories and guns and projectiles, but thousands and thousands of men, five hundred thousand, one million, one million and a half British soldiers, including your own Canadian boys, stood up and entered the fray alongside their French comrades. Such is the admirable spectacle which Great Britain presents to the wondering eyes and consciences of the world.
1 am quite aware that German calumnies must have reached this country; it is even likely that they have found their way to your minds and hearts; we do not feel humiliated because before the war you may have thought, on the faith of what was so often repeated, that France was a lost country, corrupt, dissolute, frivolous, catering solely to its pleasures, and so much rent by political dissensions that when the great struggle would come, Germany would be facing not men but a divided army, easy to scatter. Well, you have been witnesses of what France can accomplish; that wonderful France, standing undefeated because her sons keep up both with the traditions of the past and the traditions of the Revolution. You have seen what her genius can effect, the same genius that has emancipated a large se'ction of humanity. We had arms; we had an army. But what could our army do, with only 40,000,000 of inhabitants to draw from, in a struggle against the Germans who for the last 45 years have been perfecting their war machine in order to hurl it against our country. We gave way at first, both British and French; we gave way before the storm; we were not in sufficient numbers but we righted ourselves after the battle of the Marne. (Long applause,).
How has that been possible? It is because the world's estimate of France was not true.
There are political parties in France; every free democracy is made up of parties who struggle for supremacy, who hold different views, who do not servilely copy each other's gestures and expressions. What counts, after all, is that at the supreme hour all citizens unite in a common sacrifice on the altar of their country; what counts 4s that every citizen should remember that before belonging to any political party he owes allegiance to his country; as the preservation of the country is essential to the very existence of any painty. (Applause.) -
Well, what country could have done better than France to bring about this great sacred alliance? Everlastingly shall I remember, as the greatest honour that was mine in all my career, that eventful 4th of August, when I entered into the French House of Representatives with the declaration of war that had been communicated to me, as President of the French Cabinet, by Mr. de Schoen on the previous day. My colleague, the Marquis de Chambrun, a member of the French Parliament, will also recall the occurrence. There were all the members standing, quivering with emotion, all the galleries filled with wives and mothers who were going to send to the front their husbands or their sons; everybody standing; no more political parties; no more groups; none but Frenchmen reconciled in their devotion to their country. And as days followed days, all parties rallied to the same flag and put on the same uniform. Catholics no more; free-thinkers no more; Socialists no more; Radicals no more; Conservatives no more, but all children of the one France. All Frenchmen, leaving aside their old disputes, came to the common conclusion that there was no necessity to arouse political differences; that before fighting between ourselves it was first of all necessary to keep under our feet a free soil, an undivided France. As one man, we shouldered our guns, and it is that wonderful unity, that sacred unity, that has given us and will give us victory.
I join with you, Mr. Speaker, in hailing this victory. It should by all means break forth to the full knowledge of humanity; indeed, if this great effort of ours should not be crowned by victory, then I must say there never was waged a war so disastrous to the nations of the world. In former days nations have suffered grievously through defeat; but such wars were struggles between armies, and differences were settled through a treaty of peace; while in this war we are the spectators of a struggle between conflicting types of minds and nations. At present, I, repeat, What is at stake is not territorial

subtopic: THE FRENCH WAR MISSION TO THE UNITED STATES.
subsubtopic: SPECIAL, SITTING OF THE HOUSE ADDRESSED BY M. VIVIANI.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise for the purpose of making a motion-it may be allowable, although all persons sitting within this room are not members of Parliament-in order that each one who is here may give his vote thereon, silent or expressed. Would to heaven that the speech to which we have just listened, so full of heart and fire, so full of the loyal spirit that beats true to humanity's best aspirations, could have been heard by every man in our Dominion. I wish to move, Sir, that this speech, as taken down by our reporters, be inserted in the Official Report of the Debates of this Parliament, in order that it may become a part of the imperishable records of this country. Would that to those pages, which will record the words of our distinguished visitor, there could also 
be transferred the fire, the spirit, the human force and vitality which to-day have entered into those words and have given to them an import and a meaning that the printed page is all too weak to carry.
Sir, this is a most unique occasion. Have we quite an adequate sense of how unique an occasion it is? . Look at this bunting, which decorates the chamber. There are the flags of Britain, of France, of the United States of America-if we had had time, we should have had the flags of our other Allies as well. Looking at these flags on this historic occasion, what memories of the past do they invoke, what anticipations for the future! Our distinguished visitor of to-day, who has done us the extremely great honour of paying a visit to the Capital of our country, may have addressed far larger audiences and may have spoken to multitudes in comparison with which this assembly is but a smali number, but he has never had a truer response to his burning words than that which has been given him to-day by Close here assembled.
Not only have we with us to-day a man of marked personality and extreme brilliance and force of expression, but, in that chair to-day, in his personality, sits France-the France of many storied centuries, the France which, emerging from the 'dimness of past ages, has, by virile force, by artistic power, by the clear adaptation of great ideals, waged nobly and well her part of the -world's warfare and achieved her part of the world's progressive work. The representatives of that other flag have in the past fought on many a field against the representatives of the French flag. To-day those two flags are intertwined; to-day those two great nations represent one struggle, one contest for one great world-ideal of liberty and of equality. As we hear these burning words and realize that France sits there, we can see the heroic bravery of her peasant soldiery who for two years and ten months, in brown trenches and on bloody fields, have stood off the attacks of despotism, the might of German po wer and domination, and have saved not only France, but the world, and liberty, and freedom. We see, too, the unexampled heroism and the cheerful, self-denying suffering of the women of France, who, behind those trenches, have done the work formerly carried on by that soldiery, on farm, in field, and in all the avocations of life. The matchless soldiery and the devoted women of France are present with us to-day as the burning words which we have heard break upon our ears.

But, Sir, we see more than France sitting in that chair. This occasion is but the indication and registry of something wider far and deeper still which is finding birth and incarnation in the fierce struggle of to-day. Above us poises the spirit of the other mighty allied nations, whose hearts beat in unison with the heart of France and of Britain, who have caught the radiance of the same high ideal, and are pursuing it through blood and sacrifice to a victorious realization, fused together in the white heat of a fervour that burns away all previous misunderstandings, all old time feuds, all the misapprehension and ignorance of the past, and leaves the spirit of these nationalities free to knit itself together for the greater world-work which shall come after the war.
And that great work shall be the reconstruction of that which has been destroyed, the laying anew of the foundations of a world of liberty, freedom and justice; of a world which, bathed in these fires and purified in this great struggle by self-denial and sacrifice, shall be raised to higher planes, on which generations yet unborn shall flourish and flower.
And, if Canada can be allowed one small word, in that Chair we see the representative of one of the two parents of this country. Among these flags is one which is representative of Canada's other progenitor and parent. And they show you Canada, but a child, drawing its inspiration in part from France and in part from Britain, and true to the best traditions of both.
After this war, Canada can never be what she has been. The blood of her children mingles with the blood of Frenchmen and Englishmen on the soil of France. Her sympathies have been drawn towards the same ideals, comradeship has been welded in the fierce heat of battle, and a fusion of thought and sympathy and love has come which will bind this country to France and to the Allies as it never could have been bound but for the uniting power of death faced in a common cause.
It is not for me to prolong my words. Not for an instant would I attempt to set an estimation on the oration which has been delivered to us. I called it a speech* at first, but that was a feeble word by which to describe it. It was an exhibition of thought, of feeling, of fire, of high ideal and strong purpose; it was not only an exhibition of the spirit of our distinguished guest himself, but it was a translation of what his country means and is. In the
87 J
years that lie before us the memories of a great and glorious past will intertwine and play their inevitable and inexorable part, and that part can only be one of united forces making for progress and of betterment in all the long ages of the future. The old misapprehension and prejudices of the past will have passed away in the cleansing fires of war, washed away in common blood shed for a common cause, apd the spirit of our countries will emerge united for a higher ideal, and a stronger civilization.	'
In the name, Sir, of the Parliament of Canada and of the people of this country, I tender to you, Mr. Viviani, our sincere thanks for your visit to us, and for the admirable words you have spoken. This audience is small but your words, Sir, will go to the very confines of our country; they will be read by millions of people, and they will accomplish a great and beneficent work.

subtopic: THE FRENCH WAR MISSION TO THE UNITED STATES.
subsubtopic: SPECIAL, SITTING OF THE HOUSE ADDRESSED BY M. VIVIANI.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, -and may I add, though it is hardly parliamentary but justified by the occasion: Ladies and Gentlemen-a very happy thought is embodied in the motion which has just been placed in your hands by the leader of the Government. It is my honour, and still more my pleasure, to second that motion, and to that motion not only the members of Parliament here assembled but all within sound of my voice will, I am sure, be only too glad to give an unanimous assent. It was a very happy thought, indeed, that we should crystallize the events of this day in some undying manner, and what manner could be more appropriate than to incorporate in the official records of our House the message which M. Viviani has brought from the French people to the people of Canada-a message which has been expressed with eloquence unsurpassed, and in words of fire which have burned to the very core of our hearts. M. Viviani has been kind enough to say in his speech that he was bringing to us the thanks and gratitude of the French people for what we have' done for France in the present struggle. I am sure that I am voicing the feeling of every Canadian when I say that, we ask for no thanks and no gratitude. What we have done, we have done for the cause of freedom, that cause for which France has already borne such a heavy burden and made such heavy sacrifices. I am proud to say to M. Viviani that what we have done we have done willingly, freely, voluntarily,

and through no sense of compulsion. It was, indeed, the belief in many parts of the old world where the virtue of British institutions was not understood, that as soon as England became engaged in a war the result would be very different from what actually happened when this war broke out. It was the calculation of the German Emperor, of the German militarists, and of the German people, that if England became engaged in a war there would forthwith be civil war in Ireland, insurrection in India, and the British colonies would seize the opportunity to sever their connection with the Mother Country. Sir, we are not surprised that those views were entertained in Germany, because the German people have never understood the spirit of liberty. Contrary to all their calculations this paradox of an empire of free peoples has become a living thing under British institutions.
M. Viviani has also expressed to us the thanks and gratitude of the French people for the part borne by our soldiers on the battlefield. That testimony of gratitude we accept; we accept it for our noble boys who have done their part in a manner to do credit to themselves and bring glory to their country. When we faced the thought of war, there may have been those amongst us who were apprehensive as to what might be the conduct of our young soldiers, soldiers not enured to war, not previously trained for military life, and for whom the first shock of battle might be a severe ordeal. Thank the Lord, we know to-day, and it is our pride to know, that they have borne themselves in a manner which proves that the blood in their veins has not degenerated. Not only that, but more. Many of these young soldiers, our boys, who crossed the ocean, never shall re-cross it. They have shed their blood on the fields of France, their bodies lie for ever in that sacred soil. We mourn their loss. But even those who have lost them will find consolation in the thought that under the mighty scourge of war will come a union between England and France of perpetual peace and amity. These countries linked together in mutual regard are an example to the world; and, now that they have been joined by the United States, we may see in this alliance the dawn of the day long hoped for, long prayed for, but long despaired of: the realization of glory to God in the highest, peace on earth, and good will among men.

subtopic: THE FRENCH WAR MISSION TO THE UNITED STATES.
subsubtopic: SPECIAL, SITTING OF THE HOUSE ADDRESSED BY M. VIVIANI.
speechtext:
Mr. Viviani, in the person of her distinguished visitor, Canada today hails
[Sir Wilfrid Laurier.i
the official representative of France, France at all times wonderful, but who during the last three years has held and is now holding ever increasingly the world in amazement; France, of whom you have spoken with such eloquence; France, united in a sacred union, which has put an end to all feuds, differences or shades of opinion, everything that disunited her sons; and which has placed her where she stands to-day, the champion,, not only of her own freedom, but of the liberties of the world.
We greet you as the representative of France, and that greeting 'it is particularly pleasing to me to express in the French language, of which you have just spoken with such eloquence, a language which has the limpidity of a stream and the resistance of metal, which our forefathers have 'brought with them from the country of your ancestors and kept as their most, sacred heritage.
You Visited the United States, accompanied by that illustrious general. . . .
(Long applause).
by that illustrious general who at the beginning of the war had been entrusted with the destinies of France, and who was successful in 'breaking the German offensive, and destroying for ever the enemy's plans for establishing German supremacy. You have visited all the great cities, and everywhere you have, been greeted with a spontaneity, an outburst, an enthusiasm that must have sometimes astonished you and always exceeded your hopes.
You now cross from one country to another, from the land of the United States to the land of Canada, a British soil. Many are the historic ties that bind you to the United States; but stronger are those that unite you to Canada's soil; because if you have met everywhere in the United States the feeling of admiration which the mere name of France evokes here, on this British soil, you will find not only admiration, but along with our sympathy you will find national pride; you will meet two million citizens of French descent who have kept alive the cult of France, a cult, that honours France, for inspiring it, Canada for fostering it, and England for respecting it.
But I hasten to add that, if we keep up the pride of our origin, we are equally proud of our allegiance. I say our allegiance; the word has somewhat fallen into disuse in France, but it was brought from France, into England by the Normans and brought from England into Canada. We are proud of our allegiance, because wherever rights exist duties are born. We enjoy the rights of our origin, we have the duties of our allegiance, and for both we have an equal respect.

Mr. Viviani, your stay amongst us is too brief; you will soon depart; let me tell you that you leave 'behind a souvenir never to be blotted out of our memory, and that whatever happens, we shall remain true to the cause we are fighting for. We shall persevere until final victory, be that victory at hand, as we hope, or be it distant, as may *be; we are in the struggle to the end. And we have no doubt of a victorious outcome, because we, in Canada, as you, in France, have the common resolve never to lay down arms until right and justice, have again taken their place under the sun.
The DEPUTY SPEAKER [DOT]: Sir George Foster moves, seconded by Sir Wilfrid Laurier:
That the admirable and eloquent speech just delivered by M. Viviani be inserted .in the Official Report of the Debates of this House, and that it form a part o-f the permanent record of this Parliament.
Motion agreed to by a standing vote.
Hon. Sir GEORGE FOSTER moved the adjournment of the House.
He said: Before the adjournment, I beg to say that if the ladies and gentlemen present will be kind enough to walk in at the right of Mr. Speaker, and out at his left, M. Viviani will add to the gracious debt under which he has already placed us by giving them a personal greeting.
The audience then sang La Marseillaise and God Save the King, and in response to the call of the Deputy Speaker cheered " Vive la France."
Motion agreed to and House adjourned at 1.20 p.m.
Monday, May 14, 1917.
